questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus develops severe hypoglycemia and is given a glucagon rescue injection. Glucagon is released from the pancreas, travels through the bloodstream, and acts on distant hepatocytes to raise blood glucose. Which type of cell signaling does this therapy exploit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autocrine signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paracrine signaling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juxtacrine signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endocrine signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synaptic signaling

explanation.summary: Hormones carried through the blood to act on distant target cells define endocrine signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucagon is a peptide hormone secreted into the bloodstream that travels to distant hepatocytes to stimulate glucose release. Signaling that induces a response in cells at a separate, distant location via the blood is by definition endocrine signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autocrine signaling occurs when a cell secretes a ligand that binds its own receptors, not distant hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Paracrine signaling acts on nearby local cells by local diffusion, not on distant organs via the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Juxtacrine signaling requires direct physical contact between adjacent cells through gap junctions or membrane-bound ligands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synaptic signaling releases neurotransmitters across a synaptic cleft between neurons, not hormones into the blood.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with allergic asthma inhales an allergen. Mast cells in the airway wall release histamine, which acts on immediately adjacent smooth muscle and blood vessels to cause local bronchoconstriction and vasodilation. Which mode of cell signaling best describes the action of the released histamine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endocrine signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paracrine signaling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autocrine signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Synaptic signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Juxtacrine signaling

explanation.summary: A mediator that diffuses a short distance to act on nearby cells is paracrine signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Paracrine signaling propagates a signal to nearby cells. Histamine released from mast cells diffuses locally to act on adjacent smooth muscle and vascular cells, exactly the example the brick gives for paracrine inflammatory mediators.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endocrine signaling delivers hormones through the bloodstream to distant target cells, not to immediately adjacent tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autocrine signaling would require histamine to bind receptors on the same mast cell that released it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Synaptic signaling involves neurotransmitter release across a synaptic cleft between neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Juxtacrine signaling requires direct membrane contact or gap junctions rather than a diffusible mediator.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A researcher exposes a person to the nerve agent sarin. Sarin inhibits acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft, preventing hydrolysis of the neurotransmitter and leading to convulsions, paralysis, and cardiac arrest. The normal signaling process disrupted by sarin is an example of which type of cell communication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Paracrine signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endocrine signaling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Synaptic signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autocrine signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Juxtacrine signaling

explanation.summary: Neurotransmitter release across a synaptic cleft, terminated by acetylcholinesterase, defines synaptic signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Synaptic signaling occurs when chemical signals are released from a presynaptic terminal into the synaptic cleft to bind a postsynaptic membrane. Acetylcholinesterase normally terminates the signal; sarin blocks this cessation, causing sustained neurotransmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Paracrine signaling uses diffusible mediators acting on nearby cells, not neurotransmitters at a defined synapse.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endocrine signaling delivers hormones through the blood to distant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autocrine signaling occurs when a cell responds to a ligand it secreted itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Juxtacrine signaling requires direct physical contact between cells rather than a cleft-crossing transmitter.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A steroid hormone derived from cholesterol is administered to a cultured cell. Because of its chemical nature, this hormone readily crosses the plasma membrane and binds a receptor that then regulates gene transcription. Which type of receptor most likely binds this ligand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receptor tyrosine kinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: G protein-coupled receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ligand-gated ion channel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nuclear receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serine/threonine kinase receptor

explanation.summary: Lipophilic, cholesterol-derived hormones cross the membrane and act through intracellular nuclear receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Steroid hormones are lipophilic and readily cross the lipid bilayer, so they are detected by intracellular nuclear receptors that act as ligand-activated transcription factors, binding DNA to regulate gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Receptor tyrosine kinases are cell-surface receptors for polar ligands such as growth factors that cannot passively cross the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GPCRs are cell-surface receptors for hydrophilic ligands and signal through second messengers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligand-gated ion channels sit in the membrane and open in response to polar extracellular ligands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serine/threonine kinase receptors are membrane enzyme-linked receptors for peptide ligands such as TGF-beta.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A peptide hormone binds its receptor on the surface of a target cell but does not enter the cytoplasm. To generate a cellular response, the cell must produce low-molecular-weight intracellular molecules that propagate and amplify the external signal. What is the fundamental reason a peptide hormone signals in this indirect manner rather than binding an intracellular receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is hydrophilic and too large to passively cross the membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is synthesized directly from cholesterol

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is lipophilic and freely diffuses across the bilayer

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is degraded by phosphodiesterases before entering the cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an iodinated amine that binds nuclear receptors

explanation.summary: Hydrophilic, large peptide hormones cannot cross the membrane, so they use surface receptors and second messengers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peptide/protein hormones are substantially larger and polar, which along with their hydrophilic nature impedes passive diffusion into the cell. They must bind cell-surface receptors that trigger second messengers to propagate and amplify the signal internally.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholesterol-derived hormones are steroids, which are lipophilic and use nuclear receptors, unlike peptide hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptide hormones are hydrophilic, not lipophilic, and cannot freely diffuse across the bilayer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphodiesterases degrade second messengers such as cAMP, not the extracellular peptide hormone itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid hormones are iodinated amines that use nuclear receptors, but peptide hormones are a different class.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Epinephrine binds a beta-adrenergic G protein-coupled receptor. The receptor acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor on the associated Galpha subunit, which then dissociates and stimulates adenylate cyclase. Which molecule, when bound to the Galpha subunit, promotes this activation of adenylate cyclase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GDP

choices.label: B
choices.text: GTP

choices.label: C
choices.text: cAMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: ATP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inositol triphosphate (IP3)

explanation.summary: GTP-bound Galpha dissociates from the receptor and Gbeta-gamma to activate adenylate cyclase.
explanation.whyCorrect: On activation, the GPCR catalyzes exchange of GDP for GTP on Galpha. The GTP-bound Galpha subunit dissociates from the beta-gamma subunits and activates adenylate cyclase to generate cAMP, propagating the signal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GDP-bound Galpha is the inactive state formed after intrinsic GTPase hydrolysis shuts the pathway off.
whyWrongByChoice.C: cAMP is the downstream second messenger produced after Galpha activates adenylate cyclase, not the activating nucleotide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ATP is the substrate adenylate cyclase converts into cAMP, not the molecule that binds and activates Galpha.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IP3 is a second messenger of the Gq/phospholipase C pathway, not the nucleotide that activates Galpha-s.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A patient chronically consumes large amounts of caffeine, a methylxanthine that inhibits phosphodiesterase. As a result, the intracellular second messenger that normally activates protein kinase A has a prolonged half-life, sustaining alertness and increased heart rate. Which second messenger accumulates due to this phosphodiesterase inhibition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diacylglycerol (DAG)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inositol triphosphate (IP3)

choices.label: C
choices.text: cAMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nitric oxide (NO)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Calcium ions (Ca2+)

explanation.summary: Phosphodiesterases hydrolyze cyclic nucleotides; inhibiting them prolongs cAMP signaling and PKA activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: cAMP is a cyclic purine mononucleotide that activates PKA and is normally destroyed by phosphodiesterases. Caffeine inhibits PDE, prolonging the cAMP half-life to sustain downstream effects such as alertness and increased heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DAG is generated by phospholipase C cleaving PIP2 and activates PKC; it is not degraded by phosphodiesterase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IP3 is a phospholipase C product that releases calcium and is not a cyclic nucleotide targeted by phosphodiesterase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide is a gas generated from arginine; it is not a cyclic nucleotide broken down by phosphodiesterase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcium ions are released from ER/SR stores and cleared by SERCA pumps, not by phosphodiesterase.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A patient develops profuse watery diarrhea and dehydration after infection with Vibrio cholerae. Cholera toxin covalently modifies a specific Galpha subunit, preventing GTP hydrolysis so the subunit is constitutively active, leading to sustained cAMP production, PKA activation, and chloride efflux into the gut lumen. Which Galpha subunit does cholera toxin lock in the active state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Galpha-s

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galpha-i

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galpha-q

choices.label: D
choices.text: Galpha-12/13

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Gbeta-gamma complex

explanation.summary: Cholera toxin constitutively activates Galpha-s, driving unregulated cAMP production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cholera toxin covalently alters Galpha-s to prevent GTP hydrolysis, keeping it permanently active. The prolonged cAMP and PKA activity opens chloride channels; ion efflux draws water into the gut lumen, causing the severe secretory diarrhea of cholera.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Galpha-i is the target of pertussis toxin, which inhibits an inhibitor of adenylate cyclase, a different mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galpha-q activates phospholipase C to make IP3 and DAG and is not the cholera toxin target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Galpha-12/13 activates Rho kinases for cytoskeletal remodeling, unrelated to cholera toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Gbeta-gamma complex modulates ion channels such as GIRK; it is not covalently modified by cholera toxin.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Pertussis toxin from Bordetella pertussis ADP-ribosylates a Galpha subunit, effectively inhibiting an inhibitor of adenylate cyclase. This raises intracellular cAMP and impairs leukocyte function, helping the bacterium evade immune-mediated destruction. Which Galpha subunit is modified by pertussis toxin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Galpha-q

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galpha-i

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galpha-s

choices.label: D
choices.text: Galpha-12/13

choices.label: E
choices.text: RhoA

explanation.summary: Pertussis toxin inactivates Galpha-i, removing inhibition of adenylate cyclase and raising cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Galpha-i subtype normally blocks adenylate cyclase activation. Pertussis toxin modifies Galpha-i, inhibiting this inhibitor, which increases cAMP and impairs leukocyte function so the bacterium escapes immune clearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Galpha-q signals through phospholipase C to produce IP3 and DAG and is not the pertussis toxin target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galpha-s stimulates adenylate cyclase directly and is the target of cholera toxin, not pertussis toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Galpha-12/13 drives Rho-mediated cytoskeletal remodeling and is unrelated to pertussis toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RhoA is a small G-protein downstream of Galpha-12/13, not a heterotrimeric Galpha subunit modified by the toxin.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with obesity has recently developed insulin resistance and early type 2 diabetes. Insulin levels are normal or elevated, but the downstream metabolic signaling cascade is blunted. The insulin receptor is an atypical predimerized receptor tyrosine kinase whose metabolic effects depend on a PI3-kinase pathway. Which parameter is most likely decreased in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin receptor dimerization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphorylation of PKB/Akt

choices.label: D
choices.text: Synthesis of cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Activity of nuclear thyroid receptors

explanation.summary: Blunted insulin signaling reduces downstream PKB/Akt phosphorylation, impairing metabolic responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin's metabolic branch depends on PIP3-mediated recruitment and PDK1 phosphorylation of PKB/Akt. When insulin signaling is compromised, PKB/Akt activation via phosphorylation falls, reducing GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The insulin receptor is already predimerized (linked by disulfide bonds), so dimerization is not the limiting step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin is present or elevated in insulin resistance, so secretion is not decreased at onset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: cAMP is produced from GPCR-mediated signaling; the insulin receptor signals through an RTK pathway instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nuclear thyroid receptor activity is unrelated to insulin receptor tyrosine kinase signaling.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: In a research experiment, a ligand is applied to cells expressing a Gq-coupled GPCR, both with and without a SERCA inhibitor. Gq activates phospholipase C, generating IP3 and DAG; IP3 releases intracellular calcium that activates protein kinase C. Compared with cells that have functional SERCA, which parameter is most prolonged in the cells treated with the SERCA inhibitor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cAMP half-life

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protein kinase C activation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphorylation of PKB/Akt

choices.label: D
choices.text: Calmodulin inactivation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) activity

explanation.summary: SERCA normally clears cytosolic calcium; inhibiting it keeps calcium high and prolongs PKC activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gq signaling activates phospholipase C to make IP3 and DAG; IP3 releases calcium that, with DAG, activates PKC. SERCA pumps calcium back into the ER/SR to terminate the signal, so a SERCA inhibitor keeps cytosolic calcium elevated and prolongs PKC activation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: cAMP is produced by the Galpha-s/adenylate cyclase pathway, not by Gq-driven phospholipase C signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PKB/Akt phosphorylation is part of insulin receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, not Gq/calcium signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sustained high calcium would promote calmodulin activation, not inactivation, the opposite of this option.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ROCK is activated downstream of Galpha-12/13 and RhoA, not by Gq-mediated calcium release.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with stable angina places a sublingual nitroglycerine tablet under his tongue during chest pain. Nitroglycerine increases production of a gaseous signaling molecule that diffuses into vascular smooth muscle, activates cytosolic guanylate cyclase to produce cGMP, and causes vasodilation. Which molecule directly mediates this smooth muscle relaxation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nitric oxide

choices.label: B
choices.text: cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diacylglycerol (DAG)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inositol triphosphate (IP3)

explanation.summary: Nitroglycerine raises nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase to make cGMP and relax vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitric oxide is a gas that freely diffuses across membranes to activate cytosolic guanylate cyclase, producing cGMP that stimulates smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation. This relieves the pain of angina, the mechanism behind sublingual nitroglycerine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: cAMP is generated by adenylate cyclase downstream of Galpha-s and is not the gaseous mediator produced by nitroglycerine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DAG is a membrane-anchored phospholipase C product that activates PKC, not a diffusible vasodilating gas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine is a catecholamine ligand acting on adrenergic GPCRs, not the molecule generated by nitroglycerine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IP3 releases intracellular calcium and is not the gas that activates guanylate cyclase in this pathway.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man undergoes cardiac electrophysiology testing. His cardiomyocytes generate force in a coordinated fashion during each cardiac cycle because signals pass directly between physically connected adjacent cells through gap junctions. Which type of cell signaling coordinates force generation in this tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juxtacrine signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paracrine signaling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autocrine signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endocrine signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synaptic signaling

explanation.summary: Communication between physically connected cells through gap junctions or membrane-bound ligands is juxtacrine signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Juxtacrine signaling occurs when physically connected cells communicate, either via gap junctions or via membrane-bound ligands and receptors. The brick's example is cardiomyocytes coordinating force generation during a cardiac cycle through gap junctions. Endothelial-leukocyte contact via membrane-embedded adhesion molecules in chronic inflammation is another example.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Paracrine signaling uses diffusible mediators such as histamine acting on nearby cells, not direct gap-junction coupling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autocrine signaling involves a cell secreting a ligand that binds its own receptors, not communication between neighbors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endocrine signaling releases hormones into the bloodstream to act on distant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synaptic signaling releases neurotransmitter from a presynaptic terminal across a cleft, not through gap junctions.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A tumor biopsy from a 58-year-old woman with metastatic carcinoma shows that the cancer cells secrete interleukin-6 (IL-6), which binds receptors on the same cancer cells that produced it, activating signaling pathways that promote proliferation, survival, and metastasis. Which mode of cell signaling do the tumor cells use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Paracrine signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endocrine signaling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autocrine signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juxtacrine signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synaptic signaling

explanation.summary: A cell that secretes a ligand and responds to it through its own receptors is using autocrine signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autocrine signaling involves production and secretion of a ligand that binds to the cell that originally produced it. The brick's examples are activated T lymphocytes secreting growth factors that bind their own receptors, and cancer cells producing IL-6 that binds the cancer cell itself to drive proliferation, survival, and metastasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Paracrine signaling targets nearby cells that did not secrete the ligand.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endocrine signaling requires release into the bloodstream to reach distant target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Juxtacrine signaling requires physical contact via gap junctions or membrane-bound ligands, not a secreted cytokine acting on the secreting cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synaptic signaling is neurotransmitter release from a presynaptic terminal onto a postsynaptic cell.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A researcher studies a beta-2 adrenergic receptor system in cultured cells. After epinephrine is washed away, adenylate cyclase activity returns to baseline within seconds and the Galpha subunit re-associates with Gbeta-gamma and the receptor. Which event is directly responsible for turning off the activated Galpha subunit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phosphodiesterase hydrolysis of cAMP bound to the Galpha subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dissociation of the Gbeta-gamma complex from the plasma membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exchange of GDP for GTP catalyzed by the receptor's GEF activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrolysis of bound GTP to GDP by the Galpha intrinsic GTPase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phosphorylation of Galpha on tyrosine residues by protein kinase A

explanation.summary: The Galpha subunit's intrinsic GTPase hydrolyzes GTP to GDP, allowing Galpha to re-associate with Gbeta-gamma and the GPCR to turn off.
explanation.whyCorrect: Galpha has an intrinsic GTPase activity that hydrolyzes its bound GTP back to GDP. GDP-bound Galpha re-associates with the Gbeta-gamma subunits and the GPCR, shutting off downstream signaling such as adenylate cyclase activation. This is the step that bacterial toxins like cholera toxin sabotage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phosphodiesterases hydrolyze the second messenger cAMP in the cytosol; cAMP is not bound to Galpha and PDE does not inactivate Galpha.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gbeta-gamma remains membrane-associated and re-binds Galpha; its dissociation from the membrane is not the off-switch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GDP-to-GTP exchange catalyzed by the receptor acting as a GEF is the activation step, not the termination step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galpha is inactivated by GTP hydrolysis, not by tyrosine phosphorylation; PKA is a downstream effector kinase of cAMP.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman's endocrine evaluation examines two amine-derived hormones. Triiodothyronine (T3) from her thyroid gland and epinephrine from her adrenal medulla are both amine-derived, yet T3 acts through nuclear receptors while epinephrine acts through cell membrane receptors. Which property best explains this difference in receptor location?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epinephrine is synthesized as a prohormone requiring further processing

choices.label: B
choices.text: T3 is lipophilic whereas epinephrine is hydrophilic

choices.label: C
choices.text: T3 is a much larger molecule and cannot cross the plasma membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epinephrine is derived from cholesterol whereas T3 is derived from tyrosine

choices.label: E
choices.text: T3 is released into the bloodstream whereas epinephrine acts only locally

explanation.summary: Amine-derived hormones differ in solubility: thyroid hormones are lipophilic and use nuclear receptors, while catecholamines are hydrophilic and use cell membrane receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that the classes of amine-derived hormones differ in their solubility. Catecholamines such as adrenaline are hydrophilic and produced in the adrenal medulla, so they must bind cell membrane receptors. Thyroid hormones are lipophilic and readily cross the lipid bilayer, so they bind intracellular nuclear receptors, as summarized in Table 1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Synthesis as a prohormone requiring further processing is a feature of peptide/protein hormones, not catecholamines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Size is not the issue; T3 crosses the membrane readily because it is lipophilic, and it does reach nuclear receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both are amine-derived hormones synthesized from amino acids; steroids, not epinephrine, come from cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both are hormones released into the blood; the difference in receptor location reflects solubility, not distance of action.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A biochemistry student classifies hormones by their synthetic precursors and groups dopamine, serotonin, and histamine together as one class. From which precursors is this hormone class synthesized?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cholesterol via steroid synthesis pathways

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prohormones that require further processing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dietary long-chain fatty acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arachidonic acid via cyclooxygenases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Amino acids such as tyrosine and tryptophan

explanation.summary: Amine hormones are synthesized from the amino acids tyrosine, tryptophan, and histidine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 lists amine hormones as synthesized from the amino acids tyrosine, tryptophan, and histidine. Dopamine and epinephrine derive from tyrosine, serotonin from tryptophan, and histamine from histidine. Catecholamines, serotonin, and histamine are hydrophilic and use cell membrane receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholesterol is the precursor of steroid hormones such as cortisol, estrogen, and testosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Synthesis as prohormones needing further processing describes peptide/protein hormones such as insulin and prolactin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fatty acids are ligands for nuclear receptors like PPAR-alpha, not the precursors of amine hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases generate prostaglandins and leukotrienes, ligands for PPAR-gamma, not amine hormones.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man receives a drug that activates a cardiac G protein-coupled receptor. Recordings from his sinoatrial node show a dampened heart rate and reduced contractility caused by potassium ion movement through G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels that hyperpolarizes the membrane. Which G-protein component primarily regulates these channels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Galpha-s subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galpha-q subunit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galpha-12/13 subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gbeta-gamma complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small G-protein Ras

explanation.summary: GIRK channels are primarily regulated by the Gbeta-gamma subunits, whose action hyperpolarizes the membrane to dampen heart rate and contractility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond sequestering Galpha, the Gbeta-gamma complex has its own signaling roles. It can promote opening of plasma membrane cation channels, and G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels are primarily regulated by the beta-gamma subunits. The resulting potassium ion flow hyperpolarizes the membrane, producing effects such as dampened heart rate and contractility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Galpha-s activates adenylate cyclase to raise cAMP and activate PKA; it does not directly gate GIRK channels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Galpha-q activates phospholipase C to generate DAG and IP3, not potassium channel opening.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Galpha-12/13 activates Rho GEFs and RhoA/ROCK for cytoskeletal remodeling and migration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ras is a monomeric cytosolic small G-protein driving the MAP kinase cascade, not a heterotrimeric component regulating GIRK.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and obesity is started on a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist for glycemic control and weight management. The drug binds the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R). To which receptor class does GLP-1R belong, the class estimated to be the target of roughly 30-50% of all prescribed pharmacological drugs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receptor tyrosine kinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ligand-gated ion channel

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serine/threonine receptor kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nuclear receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: G protein-coupled receptor

explanation.summary: GLP-1R is a GPCR, the receptor superfamily targeted by an estimated 30-50% of prescribed drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation notes that roughly 30-50% of all prescribed pharmacological drugs target GPCRs, and that the rapidly emerging GLP-1 agonists used in diabetes and weight management act on the GLP-1 receptor, which is a GPCR. GPCRs are integral membrane receptors with 7 transmembrane domains (serpentine receptors) that activate heterotrimeric G proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RTKs bind growth factors and some hormones such as insulin and signal by tyrosine autophosphorylation, not the class of GLP-1R.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ligand-gated ion channels such as the GABA receptor pass ions in response to ligand binding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serine/threonine receptor kinases mediate pathways such as TGF-beta signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear receptors are intracellular transcription factors for hydrophobic ligands; GLP-1 is a peptide that cannot reach them.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Researchers compare activation of the heterotrimeric Galpha-s subunit with activation of the monomeric small G-protein Ras in the same cell. Both are switched on by exchange of GDP for GTP. Which feature of Ras explains why it requires a separate, distinct guanine nucleotide exchange factor rather than being activated directly by a ligand-bound receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It lacks intrinsic GTPase activity and cannot hydrolyze GTP

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is cytosolic and not physically bound to a plasma membrane receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is sequestered by Gbeta-gamma subunits until the receptor is activated

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is synthesized as an inactive prohormone requiring processing

choices.label: E
choices.text: It binds GTP only after phosphorylation by protein kinase A

explanation.summary: Small G-proteins are monomeric, cytosolic, and not bound to a GPCR, so they need their own GEF for activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monomeric, cytosolic G-proteins function similarly to the alpha subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins but are not physically bound to a GPCR. Because they are not associated with a plasma membrane receptor that could act as a GEF, they require a separate, distinct GEF for functionality. Upon mitogen stimulation, GEFs activate Ras to initiate signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ras does have GTPase activity, which allows proper regulation of growth; mutants with low GTPase activity are found in tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small G-proteins do not associate with and are not regulated by the beta-gamma subunits.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prohormone processing applies to peptide hormones, not to intracellular signaling proteins like Ras.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ras activation depends on GEF-mediated GDP/GTP exchange, not on PKA phosphorylation.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A growth factor (mitogen) binds its receptor on a fibroblast, and a GEF activates Ras. The signal is transmitted from the cell surface to the nucleus by a series of sequentially activated kinases, culminating in phosphorylated Erk entering the nucleus to activate gene transcription. Which sequence correctly orders the kinases downstream of Ras?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Raf, then MEK, then Erk

choices.label: B
choices.text: MEK, then Raf, then Erk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erk, then Raf, then MEK

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raf, then Erk, then MEK

choices.label: E
choices.text: MEK, then Erk, then Raf

explanation.summary: The MAP kinase cascade proceeds Ras to Raf to MEK to Erk, historically MAPKKK, MAPKK, and MAPK.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ras signaling is associated with the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase cascade, also called the MAPK/ERK pathway. Ras activates Raf, which activates MEK, which activates Erk. These were historically named MAP kinase kinase kinase, MAP kinase kinase, and MAP kinase; they work sequentially to carry the signal from the cell surface to the nucleus, where phosphorylated Erk activates gene transcription.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MEK is the MAP kinase kinase activated by Raf, so it cannot precede Raf.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erk is the terminal MAP kinase that enters the nucleus; it does not act upstream of Raf.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erk is activated by MEK, so MEK must precede Erk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raf is the first kinase activated by Ras (MAPKKK), not the last.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Genetic analysis of a 61-year-old man's carcinoma identifies a mutation in Ras, a finding present in about 25% of all tumors. The mutant protein drives constitutive activation of the MAP kinase cascade and unregulated proliferation. Which biochemical defect most likely characterizes this mutant Ras?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inability to bind GTP after GEF stimulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased rate of GTP hydrolysis to GDP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced intrinsic GTPase activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of the ability to activate Raf

choices.label: E
choices.text: Constitutive association with Gbeta-gamma subunits

explanation.summary: Tumor-associated Ras mutants have low GTPase activity, leaving Ras constitutively GTP-bound and active.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ras GTPase activity allows proper regulation of cellular growth by hydrolyzing GTP to return Ras to its inactive GDP-bound state. Several Ras mutants exhibit low GTPase activity, and 25% of all tumors express a constitutively active form of Ras. The name Ras comes from rat sarcoma virus, and Raf from rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A Ras that cannot bind GTP would be inactive, not constitutively active.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Faster GTP hydrolysis would shut Ras off more quickly, the opposite of constitutive activation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of Raf activation would block, not drive, the MAP kinase cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small G-proteins like Ras do not associate with or get regulated by Gbeta-gamma subunits.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A neuroscientist applies gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the major inhibitory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system, to a cultured neuron expressing GABA receptors. The neuron becomes less able to propagate signals. Which ion movement directly accounts for this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sodium influx causing depolarization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium influx causing depolarization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Potassium influx causing depolarization

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chloride influx causing hyperpolarization

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chloride efflux causing hyperpolarization

explanation.summary: Activated GABA receptors are ligand-gated ion channels that let chloride flow into the neuron, hyperpolarizing it and inhibiting signal propagation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ligand-gated ion channel receptors allow ions such as sodium, potassium, calcium, or chloride to pass through the membrane in response to ligand binding. When activated, GABA receptors allow chloride ions to flow into the neuron, causing hyperpolarization and thus inhibiting the neuron from propagating signals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sodium influx would depolarize the neuron and promote, not inhibit, signal propagation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium influx is excitatory and is not the ion carried by GABA receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GABA receptors conduct chloride, not potassium, and depolarization is the opposite of GABA's inhibitory effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GABA receptor activation moves chloride into the cell, not out of it.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: An experimental receptor tyrosine kinase carries a mutation in its extracellular domain that prevents two receptor monomers from associating after ligand binding, although each monomer's cytoplasmic kinase domain is structurally intact and ligand still binds. Which step of RTK signaling will fail first in cells expressing this mutant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ligand binding to the extracellular domain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insertion of the receptor into the plasma membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exchange of GDP for GTP on the receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binding of Gbeta-gamma subunits to the receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues on the receptor

explanation.summary: RTK activation requires ligand-induced dimerization so the monomers can autophosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues.
explanation.whyCorrect: RTK signaling is a multi-step process: ligand-induced dimerization, activation of the receptor cytoplasmic kinase domains, receptor autophosphorylation on tyrosine residues, and binding of adaptor proteins to the newly formed phosphotyrosines. Upon dimerization the monomers auto-phosphorylate each other; without dimerization, autophosphorylation cannot occur and the phosphotyrosine scaffolds that recruit intracellular signaling proteins never form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem states ligand binding still occurs; the defect is downstream at dimerization.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mutation affects monomer association, not trafficking of the receptor to the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GDP/GTP exchange is a feature of G proteins, not of receptor tyrosine kinases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gbeta-gamma subunits are part of heterotrimeric G proteins coupled to GPCRs, not RTKs.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A ligand binds an enzyme-linked cell surface receptor. Unlike a receptor tyrosine kinase, the activated receptor phosphorylates serine and threonine residues within the receptor itself. Which ligand most likely activated this receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: TGF-beta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: GABA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cortisol

explanation.summary: Serine/threonine receptor kinases, exemplified by the TGF-beta pathway, phosphorylate serine or threonine residues within the receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serine/threonine receptor kinases are similar to RTKs and are a type of enzyme-linked receptor that phosphorylates residues within the receptor, but the targeted sites are serine or threonine residues rather than tyrosines. These receptors are integral to various signaling pathways, including the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin binds a predimerized receptor tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates tyrosine residues.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine binds beta-adrenergic GPCRs, activating Galpha-s and adenylate cyclase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GABA binds a ligand-gated chloride channel, not an enzyme-linked receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol is a lipophilic steroid that binds intracellular nuclear receptors.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Adipocytes in culture are exposed to insulin in the presence of a selective phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3K) inhibitor. Insulin receptor tyrosine phosphorylation and docking of the insulin receptor substrate (IRS) remain intact. Which insulin response is most likely preserved in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell growth and DNA synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: GLUT4 translocation to the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycogen synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: PKB/Akt activation

explanation.summary: Insulin's mitogenic responses run through Ras/MAPK, whereas its metabolic responses depend on the PI3K pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin receptor signaling is segregated into two main responses. The mitogenic events (cell growth, DNA synthesis) are achieved through the Ras/MAPK pathway, while the metabolic responses (lipogenesis, glycogenesis, GLUT4 cell surface expression) depend on PI3K phosphorylating PIP2 to PIP3 and subsequent PDK1 activation of PKB/Akt. Blocking PI3K leaves the Ras/MAPK mitogenic branch intact.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT4 cell surface expression is a metabolic response downstream of PI3K and PKB/Akt, so it is lost.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogenesis is a metabolic response requiring the PI3K pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipogenesis is a PI3K-dependent metabolic response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PKB/Akt requires PIP3-mediated recruitment and PDK1 activation, which cannot occur without PI3K.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: During insulin signaling, PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 to generate PIP3 in the plasma membrane. PIP3 then serves as a docking site that recruits phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1 (PDK1) and PKB/Akt from the cytosol. Which structural feature of these cytosolic proteins allows them to bind PIP3?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tyrosine kinase domain

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA binding domain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Seven transmembrane domain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pleckstrin homology domain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ligand binding domain

explanation.summary: PIP3 creates a membrane docking site for cytosolic proteins containing pleckstrin homology (PH) domains, such as PDK1 and PKB/Akt.
explanation.whyCorrect: PIP3 creates an additional membrane docking site for cytosolic proteins containing pleckstrin homology (PH) domains, such as PDK1. PKB (also known as Akt) is another PH-containing protein that localizes to PIP3 and is activated by PDK1; once activated, PKB/Akt dissociates from the membrane to propagate the cascade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The tyrosine kinase domain is the catalytic region of the receptor, not a lipid-docking module on PDK1 or PKB.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA binding domains are features of nuclear receptors that bind regulatory DNA regions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seven transmembrane domains characterize GPCRs (serpentine receptors), not cytosolic kinases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ligand binding domain is a nuclear receptor domain that binds hydrophobic hormones.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Cortisol diffuses into a hepatocyte and binds the ligand binding domain of its intracellular receptor, which also contains a transcriptional regulation domain and a DNA binding domain. Which event occurs immediately after ligand binding that permits the receptor to induce transcription?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The receptor dimerizes and autophosphorylates on tyrosine residues

choices.label: B
choices.text: The receptor activates adenylate cyclase to generate cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: The regulatory domain dissociates after a conformational change

choices.label: D
choices.text: The receptor is cleaved by phospholipase C into two fragments

choices.label: E
choices.text: The receptor exchanges GDP for GTP at its ligand binding domain

explanation.summary: Ligand binding causes a conformational change that releases the regulatory domain so the DNA binding domain can bind its regulatory region.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nuclear receptors usually have three important domains: a transcriptional regulation domain, a DNA binding domain, and a ligand binding domain. When a ligand is bound, the receptor undergoes a conformational change so that the regulatory domain disassociates. The DNA binding domain then binds to a specific DNA regulatory region to induce transcription.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dimerization with tyrosine autophosphorylation describes RTK activation, not nuclear receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adenylate cyclase activation is a GPCR/Galpha-s event; nuclear receptors act directly on gene expression without second messengers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipase C cleaves the membrane lipid PIP2, not nuclear receptor proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GDP/GTP exchange is the activation mechanism of G proteins, not nuclear receptors.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Researchers study peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), intracellular receptors that bind DNA with RXR partners to induce transcription. PPAR-alpha is activated by fatty acids from diet and adipose tissue, and PPAR-gamma by prostaglandins and leukotrienes generated by lipoxygenases and cyclooxygenases. Which additional feature distinguishes PPARs from typical nuclear receptors such as the estrogen receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are located in the plasma membrane rather than the nucleus

choices.label: B
choices.text: They require second messengers such as cAMP to bind DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: They lack a ligand binding domain and respond only to phosphorylation

choices.label: D
choices.text: They bind hydrophilic peptide ligands via cell surface domains

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are also activated through conventional cell signaling pathways

explanation.summary: PPARs are unusual nuclear receptors activated both by traditional intracellular ligand binding and by traditional cell signaling pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that receptors like PPARs are activated both through traditional intracellular ligand binding and through the traditional cell signaling pathways discussed previously. Figure 13 illustrates this: Galpha-12/13 signaling through RhoA increases PPAR-alpha activity and fatty acid oxidation. Figure 9 shows PPAR-alpha bound by fatty acids and PPAR-gamma by prostaglandins/leukotrienes, each partnering with RXR on DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PPARs are intracellular nuclear receptors that bind DNA in the cell nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nuclear receptors, including PPARs, act as transcription factors without requiring cAMP to bind DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PPARs do bind ligands (fatty acids, prostaglandins, leukotrienes) through a ligand binding domain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only hydrophobic, membrane-permeable molecules serve as nuclear receptor ligands; PPARs do not bind peptides at the surface.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man taking a PDE-5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction asks why his heavy daily coffee consumption, which also inhibits phosphodiesterases, has never produced a similar effect. Which explanation is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Caffeine raises cAMP, which directly inhibits guanylate cyclase in the corpus cavernosum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caffeine inhibits cAMP-degrading PDE isoforms distinct from PDE-5, which eliminates cGMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Caffeine is a methylxanthine that cannot cross the plasma membrane of vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Caffeine's adenosine receptor blockade cancels out its phosphodiesterase inhibition in all tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Caffeine's phosphodiesterase inhibition is limited to cardiac tissue by drug compartmentalization

explanation.summary: PDE isoform selectivity explains the difference: caffeine inhibits cAMP-degrading isoforms, whereas PDE-5 selectively eliminates cGMP in the corpus cavernosum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical reasoning explains that the answer lies in drug compartmentalization and PDE isoforms. The PDE isoforms that degrade cAMP and are inhibited by caffeine are distinct from PDE-5, which selectively eliminates cGMP in the corpus cavernosum of the penis. Sildenafil's effect depends on prolonging cGMP, a second messenger caffeine's PDE targets do not control.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick does not describe cAMP inhibiting guanylate cyclase; the distinction is which cyclic nucleotide each PDE isoform hydrolyzes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caffeine acts intracellularly on PDEs; membrane impermeability is not the reason it lacks a PDE-5-like effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenosine receptor blockade is an additional caffeine mechanism, not a cancellation of its PDE inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Caffeine's PDE inhibition sustains alertness and cognition as well as heart rate; it is isoform selectivity, not cardiac restriction, that matters.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Two receptors on the same hepatocyte both act on the membrane lipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2): a Gq-coupled receptor for one hormone and the insulin receptor. Compared with the Gq pathway, how does insulin receptor signaling utilize PIP2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It hydrolyzes PIP2 into IP3 and DAG via phospholipase C

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cleaves PIP2 to release calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: C
choices.text: It phosphorylates PIP2 to form PIP3 as a membrane docking site

choices.label: D
choices.text: It converts PIP2 into cAMP via adenylate cyclase

choices.label: E
choices.text: It dephosphorylates PIP2 to phosphatidylinositol via phosphodiesterase

explanation.summary: The same lipid PIP2 is phosphorylated by PI3K to PIP3 in insulin signaling but hydrolyzed by PLC into IP3 and DAG in Gq signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: IP3 and DAG are produced from hydrolysis of PIP2 via phospholipase C in Gq signaling. The brick stresses that this is the same phosphorylated lipid used by insulin signaling as a substrate of PI 3-kinase, which instead phosphorylates it to PIP3 to generate a docking site for pleckstrin homology domain proteins. Figure 10 summarizes the two distinct fates of PIP2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrolysis by phospholipase C into IP3 and DAG is the Gq pathway, not the insulin pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium release from ER/SR stores is triggered by IP3, a product of the Gq/PLC pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: cAMP is synthesized from ATP by adenylate cyclase downstream of Galpha-s, not from PIP2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphodiesterases hydrolyze cyclic nucleotides; the brick describes no PDE-mediated dephosphorylation of PIP2.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: Following activation of phospholipase C in a cell, two second messengers are generated from the same membrane lipid. One diffuses rapidly through the cytoplasm to bind the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, while the other remains anchored in the plasma membrane. Which structural difference accounts for this behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IP3 is a triply phosphorylated carbohydrate, whereas DAG retains glycerol with two fatty acid chains

choices.label: B
choices.text: IP3 retains glycerol with two fatty acid chains, whereas DAG is a triply phosphorylated carbohydrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: IP3 is a cyclic purine mononucleotide, whereas DAG is a serine/threonine kinase anchored in the membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: IP3 remains bound to the Gbeta-gamma complex, whereas DAG remains bound to the Galpha-q subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: IP3 is a freely diffusible gas derived from arginine, whereas DAG is an ion that requires a channel

explanation.summary: IP3 is a water-soluble carbohydrate with three phosphates that diffuses in the cytosol, while DAG is a glycerol with two fatty acid chains anchored in the membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: IP3 is a carbohydrate with 3 phosphates; therefore it is highly water soluble and diffusible within the cytoplasm, binding the ER membrane (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle) to trigger calcium release. In contrast, DAG contains a glycerol with two fatty acid chains and is anchored to the plasma membrane, where it activates PKC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the two structures: the fatty acid-containing glycerol is DAG, and the phosphorylated carbohydrate is IP3.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyclic purine mononucleotides are cAMP and cGMP; DAG is a lipid, not a kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither IP3 nor DAG remains bound to G-protein subunits; they are released products of PLC cleavage of PIP2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitric oxide is the gas derived from arginine; DAG is a lipid, not an ion.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 22-year-old sprinter's biceps contracts during a race. Nerve impulses raise intracellular calcium in her skeletal muscle fibers, and glycogen degradation rapidly increases to fuel contraction. Which sequence links the calcium rise to glycogen breakdown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium activates protein kinase C, which phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase directly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium binds calmodulin, activating phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calcium binds SERCA, activating protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Calcium activates guanylate cyclase, and the resulting cGMP phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Calcium binds calmodulin, which removes the inhibitory phosphate from glycogen phosphorylase to activate it

explanation.summary: In contracting skeletal muscle, calcium-calmodulin activates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase to its active form and drives glycogen degradation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Calcium can be released by stimuli such as nerve conduction associated with skeletal muscle contraction. As shown in Figure 11, the nerve impulse raises calcium, which binds calmodulin; calcium-calmodulin activates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates inactive glycogen phosphorylase to its active form, prompting glycogen degradation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PKC is activated by calcium with DAG in Gq signaling; the muscle glycogen pathway runs through calmodulin and phosphorylase kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SERCA is the Ca-ATPase that terminates calcium signals by pumping calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not a calcium sensor that activates PKA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Guanylate cyclase is activated by nitric oxide, and cGMP is a second messenger, not a kinase that phosphorylates proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylation, not by removal of a phosphate; the inactive form is dephosphorylated.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A researcher stimulates a GPCR coupled to Galpha-12/13 in cultured leukocytes and observes remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton with increased cell movement and migration. Which sequence of events mediates this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Galpha-12/13 activates phospholipase C, generating IP3 and DAG that activate PKC

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galpha-12/13 activates adenylate cyclase, generating cAMP that activates PKA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galpha-12/13 activates Rho GEFs, generating GTP-bound RhoA that activates ROCK

choices.label: D
choices.text: Galpha-12/13 opens GIRK channels, hyperpolarizing the membrane to trigger motility

choices.label: E
choices.text: Galpha-12/13 activates Ras, generating the Raf-MEK-Erk cascade that activates ROCK

explanation.summary: Galpha-12/13 signals through Rho GEFs to RhoA, which activates the serine-threonine kinase ROCK to remodel the actin cytoskeleton.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 12,13 subtype entails activation of Rho kinases that lead to cytoskeletal remodeling to promote cell movement and migration. The mechanism for Galpha-12/13 signaling to RhoA is through activation of Rho GEFs. GTP-bound RhoA in turn activates Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK), a serine-threonine protein kinase that regulates cell shape and movement by acting on the actin cytoskeleton.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phospholipase C activation with IP3/DAG production is the Galpha-q pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adenylate cyclase activation and cAMP/PKA signaling is the Galpha-s pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GIRK channels are regulated by Gbeta-gamma subunits and dampen heart rate; they are not the Galpha-12/13 mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ras and the Raf-MEK-Erk cascade drive gene transcription in response to mitogens; ROCK is activated by RhoA, not Erk.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A researcher studies macrophages that kill engulfed bacteria by producing a gaseous signaling molecule. The same molecule inhibits platelet aggregation, acts as a neurotransmitter, and relaxes vascular smooth muscle through cytosolic guanylate cyclase. From which precursor is this molecule synthesized?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amino acid arginine, with oxygen

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amino acid tyrosine, with iodine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cholesterol, with oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Guanosine triphosphate, by guanylate cyclase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adenosine triphosphate, by adenylate cyclase

explanation.summary: Nitric oxide is derived from the amino acid arginine and oxygen and has bactericidal, antiplatelet, neurotransmitter, and vasodilatory roles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitric oxide (NO) is a gas that freely diffuses across membranes to activate cytosolic guanylate cyclase. Figure 12 shows that membrane-soluble NO is derived from the amino acid arginine plus oxygen, generated through receptor-mediated stimulation or nerve impulses. Besides vasodilation, NO has bactericidal activity in macrophages, inhibits platelet aggregation, and is a neurotransmitter.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tyrosine with iodine gives rise to thyroid hormones, which are lipophilic amine hormones acting on nuclear receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholesterol is the precursor of steroid hormones, not of nitric oxide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GTP is the substrate guanylate cyclase converts to cGMP after NO activates the enzyme; it is not the source of NO.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ATP is converted to cAMP by adenylate cyclase in Galpha-s signaling, unrelated to NO synthesis.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: In a cell stimulated through a Gq-coupled receptor, phospholipase C produces DAG and IP3. An experimental compound prevents DAG from interacting with protein kinase C, while IP3-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum remains normal. Which effect on protein kinase C is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PKC is unaffected because calmodulin substitutes for DAG in PKC activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: PKC is hyperactivated because DAG normally inhibits its calcium binding

choices.label: C
choices.text: PKC is degraded because DAG protects it from phosphodiesterases

choices.label: D
choices.text: PKC translocates to the nucleus and binds DNA regulatory regions

choices.label: E
choices.text: PKC activation is reduced because its affinity for calcium is not increased

explanation.summary: DAG activates PKC by increasing its affinity for calcium, which IP3 makes available; without DAG, PKC activation is blunted despite normal calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: DAG, anchored to the plasma membrane, activates PKC by increasing its affinity for calcium, which is readily available due to the action of IP3. The two second messengers cooperate: IP3 supplies the calcium and DAG makes PKC responsive to it. Blocking the DAG-PKC interaction therefore reduces PKC activation even though calcium release is intact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calmodulin is a separate calcium-binding effector; the brick does not describe it substituting for DAG in PKC activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DAG increases, not inhibits, PKC's calcium affinity, so its loss reduces rather than enhances activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phosphodiesterases hydrolyze cyclic nucleotides like cAMP and cGMP; they do not degrade PKC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Binding DNA regulatory regions is the function of nuclear receptors, not of PKC.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease and symptomatic anemia is started on epoetin (recombinant erythropoietin) to stimulate red blood cell production. Erythropoietin binds a receptor that lacks intrinsic catalytic activity. Through which of the following mechanisms does this receptor most likely propagate its intracellular signal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intrinsic receptor autophosphorylation on cytoplasmic tyrosines

choices.label: B
choices.text: An associated Janus kinase that phosphorylates STAT proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: A G-alpha-s subunit that activates adenylate cyclase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptor kinase phosphorylation of SMAD transcription factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: IKK-mediated phosphorylation and degradation of IkB

explanation.summary: Cytokine receptors such as the EPO receptor lack intrinsic kinase activity and rely on Janus kinases (JAKs) to phosphorylate STATs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The EPO receptor is a hematopoietic cytokine receptor without catalytic activity of its own. Ligand binding brings associated JAKs into proximity so they phosphorylate the receptor and then STAT proteins, which dimerize and translocate to the nucleus to act as transcription factors driving RBC differentiation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intrinsic autophosphorylation describes receptor tyrosine kinases (e.g., the EGF receptor), which possess catalytic activity the EPO receptor lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G-alpha-s activation of adenylate cyclase is a GPCR/cAMP mechanism, not the cytokine-receptor pathway used by EPO.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SMAD phosphorylation is characteristic of serine/threonine receptor kinases such as the TGF-beta receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IKK-mediated IkB degradation liberates NF-kB and is downstream of TNF-alpha, not EPO.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studies how oxygen availability controls erythropoietin (EPO) production. Under well-oxygenated (normoxic) conditions, EPO gene expression is kept low. Which of the following best explains why EPO levels remain low when tissue oxygen is normal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HIF-1-alpha is hydroxylated, bound by VHL, and degraded by the proteasome

choices.label: B
choices.text: HIF-1-alpha dimerizes with HIF-beta and binds the hypoxia response element

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolyl hydroxylases are inactivated, stabilizing HIF-1-alpha

choices.label: D
choices.text: JAK2 constitutively phosphorylates STAT independent of ligand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gene amplification increases the number of EPO gene copies

explanation.summary: In normoxia, oxygen-dependent prolyl hydroxylases mark HIF-1-alpha for VHL-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, keeping EPO low.
explanation.whyCorrect: When oxygen is abundant, prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs) hydroxylate HIF-1-alpha. Hydroxylated HIF-1-alpha is recognized by the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) protein, which promotes ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, preventing transcription of hypoxia genes like EPO.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dimerization of HIF-1-alpha with HIF-beta at the hypoxia response element occurs during hypoxia to raise EPO, not in normoxia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PHDs are oxygen-dependent and active in normoxia; their inactivation stabilizes HIF-1-alpha and occurs during hypoxia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Constitutive JAK2 signaling describes polycythemia vera, not the normal oxygen-sensing regulation of EPO.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gene amplification is an overexpression mechanism seen in cancers such as HER2+ breast cancer, not physiologic EPO regulation.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man reports intense itching after hot showers, facial redness, and headaches. Laboratory studies show an elevated red blood cell count, and genetic testing identifies a JAK2 V617F mutation. This mutation causes constitutive signaling that mimics the binding of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibroblast growth factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transforming growth factor-beta

explanation.summary: Polycythemia vera results from a JAK2 mutation that constitutively activates the JAK-STAT pathway normally triggered by erythropoietin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical picture—elevated RBCs, aquagenic pruritus, plethora—is polycythemia vera, driven by JAK2 V617F. Because JAK2 relays erythropoietin signaling to promote RBC production, constitutive JAK2 activity mimics ongoing EPO stimulation even without ligand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TNF-alpha activates the NF-kB inflammatory cascade, not the erythropoietic JAK2/STAT pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblast growth factor acts through FGFR-3 in bone growth (achondroplasia), unrelated to RBC overproduction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-MSH signals through MC1R/cAMP for melanin production, not JAK2-driven erythropoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta signals through SMAD proteins and is not the ligand relayed by JAK2 in erythropoiesis.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presents with fatigue, splenomegaly, and a markedly elevated white blood cell count. Cytogenetics reveal a t(9;22) translocation. The resulting fusion gene produces a protein that drives his disease. Which of the following best describes the pathologic protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An overexpressed receptor tyrosine kinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: A constitutively active nonreceptor cytosolic tyrosine kinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: A constitutively active G-alpha-s subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: A transcription factor with a phosphomimetic substitution

choices.label: E
choices.text: A soluble decoy receptor lacking intracellular signaling

explanation.summary: The Philadelphia chromosome fuses BCR and ABL, yielding a constitutively active nonreceptor tyrosine kinase that drives chronic myeloid leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The t(9;22) translocation joins the ABL gene—encoding a freely diffusible cytosolic (nonreceptor) tyrosine kinase—to BCR. The BCR-ABL fusion retains full kinase activity but loses regulatory sites, causing constitutive pro-growth signaling and CML.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABL is explicitly not a receptor tyrosine kinase; it is a cytoplasmic protein, and the defect is a fusion, not overexpression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A constitutively active G-alpha-s subunit characterizes McCune-Albright syndrome, not CML.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The BCR-ABL defect is a gross structural fusion, not a single phosphomimetic amino-acid substitution in a transcription factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A soluble decoy receptor describes etanercept, a therapeutic, not the leukemogenic fusion protein.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cancer biologist studies a colon epithelial cell in which Wnt binds the Frizzled receptor, activating the intracellular component Dishevelled. Which of the following is the most direct downstream consequence of Dishevelled activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of the Axin/APC/GSK-3-beta destruction complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autophosphorylation of Frizzled on cytoplasmic tyrosine residues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphorylation of STAT proteins by Janus kinases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Degradation of IkB to release NF-kB into the nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased transbinding of E-cadherin between adjacent cells

explanation.summary: In Wnt signaling, Dishevelled inhibits the beta-catenin destruction complex, allowing beta-catenin to accumulate and enter the nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: When Wnt binds Frizzled (a GPCR), Dishevelled is activated and inhibits the complex of Axin, APC, GSK-3-beta, and CKI-alpha that normally targets beta-catenin for degradation. By 'inhibiting the inhibitor,' free beta-catenin translocates to the nucleus to promote gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Frizzled is a GPCR without intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, so it does not autophosphorylate like an RTK.
whyWrongByChoice.C: STAT phosphorylation by JAKs is part of the cytokine JAK-STAT pathway, not Wnt/Frizzled signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IkB degradation releasing NF-kB is the TNF-alpha inflammatory cascade, unrelated to Dishevelled.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wnt signaling frees beta-catenin for migration-promoting transcription; increased E-cadherin transbinding instead sequesters beta-catenin at the membrane.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with early pubic hair, a growth spurt placing him at the 97th height percentile, enlarged testicles, and hyperpigmented macules on his torso. Imaging shows craniofacial fibrous dysplasia. Genetic testing points to a somatic mutation in a cell-signaling gene. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiologic mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Constitutive G-alpha-s activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activating mutation of fibroblast growth factor receptor-3

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression of a BCR-ABL fusion protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of erythropoietin expression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Amplification of a receptor tyrosine kinase gene

explanation.summary: McCune-Albright syndrome arises from a somatic GNAS mutation that constitutively activates G-alpha-s, overstimulating adenylate cyclase and cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The triad of precocious puberty, cafe-au-lait spots, and fibrous dysplasia is McCune-Albright syndrome. A somatic (non-inherited) mutation in GNAS locks G-alpha-s in the active state, overproducing cAMP and driving excessive hormone synthesis and abnormal bone and pigment cell behavior.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An activating FGFR-3 mutation causes achondroplasia (short-limbed dwarfism), not precocious puberty with fibrous dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A BCR-ABL fusion causes leukemia through an abnormal tyrosine kinase, not this endocrine/skeletal picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of EPO expression would cause anemia and does not match these findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RTK gene amplification drives cancers such as HER2+ breast cancer, not McCune-Albright syndrome.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has disproportionately short upper arms and thighs, a long narrow trunk, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, and normal cognitive development. The condition results from an activating mutation in a receptor tyrosine kinase. Which of the following best explains the short stature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced chondrocyte proliferation accelerating endochondral ossification

choices.label: B
choices.text: FGFR-3 signaling that suppresses chondrocyte proliferation and cartilage formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deficient intramembranous ossification of the skull and ribs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Constitutive JAK2 activation impairing bone marrow output

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss-of-function of G-alpha-s reducing cAMP in osteoblasts

explanation.summary: Achondroplasia is caused by an activating FGFR-3 mutation that suppresses chondrocyte proliferation, limiting the cartilage-based (endochondral) growth of long bones.
explanation.whyCorrect: In achondroplasia, gain-of-function FGFR-3 autophosphorylates without ligand. FGFR-3 signaling suppresses chondrocyte differentiation and proliferation, decreasing cartilage formation needed for endochondral ossification of the long bones, producing rhizomelic shortening with preserved intelligence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FGFR-3 activation suppresses—rather than enhances—chondrocyte proliferation, so bone growth is inhibited.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flat bones like the skull form by intramembranous ossification, which is relatively preserved; the defect impairs endochondral ossification of long bones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: JAK2 activation drives polycythemia vera, not the skeletal phenotype of achondroplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Achondroplasia is a gain-of-function RTK mutation, not a loss of G-alpha-s/cAMP signaling.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A pathologist evaluates a breast tumor that is classified as HER2-positive. HER2 is a pro-growth receptor tyrosine kinase. Which of the following mechanisms most commonly accounts for the increased HER2 signaling in this cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A phosphomimetic substitution stabilizing the active receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gene amplification producing extra HER2 gene copies

choices.label: C
choices.text: A chromosomal translocation creating a fusion protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Altered epigenetic imprinting silencing the receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: A promoter mutation that decreases transcription

explanation.summary: HER2-positive breast cancer results from amplification/duplication of the HER2 gene, overexpressing a pro-growth RTK.
explanation.whyCorrect: Overexpression can amplify a pro-growth pathway, and in HER2+ breast cancer the receptor is overproduced due to an increased number of HER2 gene copies (gene amplification/duplication). This excessive receptor density drives uncontrolled proliferative signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A phosphomimetic substitution is an activating point mutation; HER2+ cancer reflects overexpression from extra gene copies, not a mimic of phosphorylation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A translocation-derived fusion protein describes BCR-ABL in leukemia, not HER2 amplification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epigenetic silencing would reduce, not increase, receptor levels, opposite to the overexpression seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A promoter mutation that decreases transcription would lower HER2, whereas the disease is defined by overexpression.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: In a macrophage, TNF-alpha binds TNFR-1 and triggers the NF-kB cascade. The NF-kB complex is normally held inactive in the cytoplasm. Which of the following events most directly liberates NF-kB so it can translocate to the nucleus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dimerization and nuclear translocation of STAT proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: IKK-mediated phosphorylation of IkB, marking it for proteasomal degradation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolyl hydroxylation of NF-kB by oxygen-dependent enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphorylation of SMAD proteins by an activated receptor kinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of the Axin/APC/GSK-3-beta destruction complex

explanation.summary: NF-kB is sequestered by IkB; IKK phosphorylates IkB, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, freeing NF-kB.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inhibitor of kappa-B (IkB) keeps NF-kB in the cytoplasm. Upon receptor activation, the IkB kinase (IKK) complex phosphorylates IkB, a post-translational mark that leads to its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, releasing NF-kB (p50/p65) to enter the nucleus and induce gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: STAT dimerization is the JAK-STAT pathway, not the mechanism releasing NF-kB.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prolyl hydroxylation regulates HIF-1-alpha in oxygen sensing, not NF-kB liberation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SMAD phosphorylation belongs to TGF-beta serine/threonine receptor signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting the destruction complex frees beta-catenin in Wnt signaling, not NF-kB.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed etanercept, a recombinant protein resembling the shed, proteolytically cleaved TNFR-1. Which of the following best describes how etanercept reduces inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a monoclonal antibody that opsonizes synovial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It acts as a soluble decoy that binds TNF-alpha

choices.label: C
choices.text: It phosphorylates IkB to prevent NF-kB release

choices.label: D
choices.text: It blocks the ATP-binding pocket of intracellular tyrosine kinases

choices.label: E
choices.text: It increases membrane-bound TNFR-1 to enhance signaling

explanation.summary: Etanercept is a soluble decoy receptor that intercepts TNF-alpha before it engages membrane receptors, dampening NF-kB-driven inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Etanercept mimics the shed soluble TNFR-1. Because it is not membrane-bound, it binds circulating TNF-alpha but cannot transduce an intracellular signal, preventing the cytokine from engaging cell-surface receptors and thereby reducing immune-related gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Etanercept is a recombinant decoy receptor, not a monoclonal antibody (that description fits adalimumab).
whyWrongByChoice.C: It sequesters extracellular TNF-alpha; it does not act intracellularly to phosphorylate IkB.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking a kinase ATP pocket describes small-molecule inhibitors like imatinib, not etanercept.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Etanercept intercepts TNF-alpha to reduce signaling; it does not increase membrane TNFR-1.

questions.topicName: Overview of Cell Signaling (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A neonate has delayed separation of the umbilical cord, recurrent skin and mucosal infections, and notably absent pus formation at sites of infection. The condition is caused by a defect in an adhesion molecule required for neutrophils to exit blood vessels. Which of the following molecules is most likely defective?

choices.label: A
