questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia is found to have a small pancreatic tumor consistent with an insulinoma. Which of the following best characterizes insulin secretion from the tumor cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It occurs only when blood glucose is elevated

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is suppressed by GLUT2-mediated glucose entry

choices.label: C
choices.text: It occurs independent of blood glucose levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires exogenous recombinant insulin priming

choices.label: E
choices.text: It yields insulin that lacks the C-peptide

explanation.summary: Insulinoma cells have lost the glucose-dependent regulation of secretion, releasing insulin regardless of blood glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: An insulinoma is a rare pancreatic tumor that overproduces insulin. The cellular transformation disrupts the regulation governing insulin secretion, so insulin secretion from the tumor cells occurs independent of blood glucose levels. This is why hypoglycemia develops, and these patients typically have high circulating C-peptide levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucose-dependent release is the normal beta-cell behavior that the tumor has lost.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose entry through GLUT2 normally stimulates secretion; it does not suppress it, and the tumor has escaped this control anyway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The tumor produces insulin endogenously; no exogenous insulin is involved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endogenous insulin from an insulinoma is processed normally and is accompanied by high C-peptide.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man rescued after weeks without food is given a large carbohydrate-rich meal. Several hours later he develops generalized weakness and a cardiac arrhythmia, and his serum potassium is found to be markedly low. Which of the following best explains the fall in serum potassium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dietary glucose binds potassium in the gut and blocks absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Refeeding increases glomerular filtration and renal potassium loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thiamin deficiency prevents renal reabsorption of potassium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Breakdown of starved tissue releases potassium into the urine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin secretion traps potassium inside cells throughout the body

explanation.summary: Refeeding triggers insulin secretion, which drives potassium into cells body-wide, producing hypokalemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Upon reintroduction of glucose after prolonged dietary absence, insulin secretion is triggered, trapping potassium inside the pancreatic cells and many other cell types and driving potassium into cells throughout the body. This shift in equilibrium results in hypokalemia, which can spawn arrhythmias, general weakness, neurological maladies, and a spectrum of other organ dysfunction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Refeeding hypokalemia is a redistribution from extracellular to intracellular fluid, not a failure of absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mechanism is compartment shift into cells, not urinary loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thiamin deficiency in refeeding causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, not renal potassium handling defects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Refeeding stimulates anabolism, not catabolism, and the potassium moves into cells rather than out to the urine.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A severely malnourished 20-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted for nutritional rehabilitation. Before any feeding, her serum potassium, phosphate, and magnesium are all at the low end of the normal range. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of these values?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Body stores are adequate, so feeding can start without monitoring

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blunted metabolism masks depletion; levels will drop with feeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-normal values exclude the risk of re-feeding syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum values mirror intracellular stores, which are also normal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Levels will climb further once anabolic pathways resume

explanation.summary: Low-normal pre-feeding electrolytes are deceptive in starvation; once metabolic demand returns, a rapid intracellular shift can be lethal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Even in a severely malnourished individual, serum potassium, phosphate, and magnesium can appear at the low end of normal. This is deceptive because tissue metabolism is severely blunted in the nutrient-deprived state. Once metabolic demands increase with reintroduction of food, insulin signaling stimulates long-dormant protein translation and glycogen synthesis, and the rapid shift of these micronutrients into cells can be lethal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Strict monitoring with phased reintroduction is exactly what these patients require.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normal-appearing values are the expected pre-feeding picture in patients who go on to develop the syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum values are misleading precisely because demand is suppressed; they do not certify intracellular sufficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resumption of anabolism pulls these ions into cells, lowering serum levels rather than raising them.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A medical team plans nutrition for an emaciated prisoner liberated after months of severe deprivation. Which of the following approaches best prevents re-feeding syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phased reintroduction of nutrients, electrolytes, and vitamins with strict monitoring

choices.label: B
choices.text: An immediate large bolus of carbohydrate-rich food to restore anabolism quickly

choices.label: C
choices.text: A priming dose of insulin before the first meal to speed glucose uptake

choices.label: D
choices.text: Withholding all electrolytes and vitamins until blood glucose normalizes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intravenous dextrose alone, given continuously until appetite returns

explanation.summary: Re-feeding must be carefully planned in phases and levels with strict monitoring of fluids, electrolytes, and vitamins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe malnutrition is not resolved by merely reintroducing a bolus of food to promote anabolism via insulin. Reintroduction of nutrients including select fluids, electrolytes, and vitamins is carefully planned in phases and levels with strict monitoring. The Bergen-Belsen liberation, where well-meaning soldiers gave rations to starving captives who then died, illustrates the danger of uncontrolled refeeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A large carbohydrate bolus triggers the insulin surge that causes lethal shifts of potassium, phosphate, and magnesium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Additional insulin would intensify the intracellular shift of micronutrients that defines the syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Electrolytes and vitamins such as thiamin are precisely what must be supplied and monitored, not withheld.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose reintroduced without thiamin and electrolyte management precipitates the syndrome, including Wernicke-Korsakoff.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A severely malnourished 8-year-old child is admitted with multiple laboratory abnormalities. Carefully phased refeeding is begun. Which of the following abnormalities present at admission is expected to improve rather than worsen as refeeding proceeds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypophosphatemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypokalemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypomagnesemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypoalbuminemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamin deficiency

explanation.summary: Hypoalbuminemia reflects the nutrient-deprived state and is corrected by refeeding-stimulated protein synthesis, unlike the electrolyte and thiamin problems that refeeding aggravates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypoalbuminemia is associated with nutrient-deprived states such as Kwashiorkor. Refeeding stimulates insulin-driven protein translation, so albumin synthesis resumes and the decrement in protein synthesis resolves. In contrast, the intracellular shift of potassium, phosphate, and magnesium and the surge in thiamin demand are all made worse by reintroducing glucose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phosphate rushes into cells to support glycolysis and kinase signaling during refeeding, so hypophosphatemia worsens.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin secretion traps potassium inside cells, deepening hypokalemia with refeeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Magnesium is consumed by insulin-stimulated metabolic processes, so serum levels fall further.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Refeeding glucose increases demand for thiamin as a PDH cofactor and can precipitate Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man subjected to prolonged starvation dies of a respiratory infection that would ordinarily be trivial in a well-nourished adult. Which of the following best explains his susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess insulin suppresses glucose uptake by leukocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glycogen release causes hyperglycemia that impairs neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of body protein compromises immune function

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sustained AMPK activity blocks antibody secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protein-fueled gluconeogenesis accelerates late in the fast

explanation.summary: In prolonged starvation, vital protein is progressively lost, and immune function is compromised by the lack of protein integrity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although protein degradation to support gluconeogenesis slows in prolonged starvation compared with the first days, vital protein from tissues is still being lost. If prolonged, proteins are depleted to the point that vital tissues like the heart fail, and normal responses such as immune function are compromised by a lack of protein integrity. Nutrient-deprived individuals may therefore succumb to infections that are normally not a concern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Starvation is a low-insulin state; insulin excess is not the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prolonged starvation depletes glycogen and produces low, not high, blood glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AMPK promotes catabolism in low-energy states; the brick does not attribute immune failure to AMPK.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein degradation for gluconeogenesis slows, not accelerates, during prolonged starvation.

questions.topicName: Cell Signaling in Context: Fed and Fasting Metabolic State (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A committee is setting nutrient intake guidance for a newly recognized micronutrient. There is not enough scientific evidence to calculate a value that meets the requirement of 50% of healthy individuals, so they instead rely on observed and experimentally approximated intakes of healthy population groups. Which dietary reference intake value are they establishing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adequate Intake (AI)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dietary Reference Intake (DRI)

explanation.summary: Adequate Intake (AI) is used when an EAR cannot be determined.
explanation.whyCorrect: AI is a value based on observed or experimentally determined approximations of nutrient intake by groups of healthy people. It is set in lieu of an RDA when there is insufficient evidence to calculate an EAR, exactly the scenario described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The EAR is a defined value meeting the requirement of 50% of healthy individuals; the committee could not calculate it here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The RDA is derived from the EAR and covers 97-98% of individuals, so it also cannot be set without an EAR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The UL is the safety ceiling for adverse effects, not a value for planning adequate intake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DRI is the umbrella term for the entire set of reference values, not the specific value being established.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in a region where maize is the dietary staple presents with a symmetric, hyperpigmented, scaly rash over sun-exposed skin of the arms and a collar-like rash around the neck. He also reports diarrhea, and his family notes progressive confusion and irritability. Deficiency of which vitamin best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin B1 (thiamin)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin B3 (niacin)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B9 (folate)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)

explanation.summary: Pellagra from niacin (B3) deficiency causes dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Niacin deficiency produces pellagra, defined by the 4 D's: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated. The photosensitive dermatitis in sun-exposed areas with the collar-like Casal necklace is classic, and it is historically common in corn-based diets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thiamin deficiency causes beriberi with cardiomyopathy and peripheral neuropathy, not a photosensitive rash with the 4 D's.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and neurologic symptoms, not pellagra.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia or birth defects, not the pellagra triad.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding gums and pinpoint hemorrhages, not the Casal necklace.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with a pellagra-like photosensitive rash and intermittent cerebellar ataxia. Laboratory studies show a marked increase in neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, in the urine, while plasma amino acid levels are low. The underlying defect involves a transporter in the intestine and kidney. Which condition most likely accounts for this patient's niacin deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carcinoid syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hartnup disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolonged isoniazid therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Biotinidase deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Classic phenylketonuria (PKU)

explanation.summary: Hartnup disease impairs tryptophan absorption, reducing niacin availability.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hartnup disease is a defective neutral amino acid transporter in the intestine and kidney. Tryptophan fails to be absorbed and is lost in the urine; because tryptophan can be catabolized to nicotinamide for NAD+, this decrement can culminate in pellagra.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carcinoid syndrome depletes tryptophan by shunting it into excess serotonin synthesis, not by a defective amino acid transporter with aminoaciduria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isoniazid depletes vitamin B6 needed to synthesize niacin, but it does not cause neutral aminoaciduria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biotinidase deficiency impairs biotin recycling and causes a biotin, not niacin, deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PKU results from defective phenylalanine hydroxylase and does not cause tryptophan wasting or pellagra.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a long history of chronic alcohol use is admitted with dilated cardiomyopathy and high-output heart failure along with a symmetric peripheral sensory neuropathy. His symptoms improve rapidly after intravenous administration of a specific vitamin. This vitamin's active cofactor is required by transketolase and by pyruvate dehydrogenase. Which vitamin was administered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin B1 (thiamin)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B3 (niacin)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B7 (biotin)

explanation.summary: Thiamin (B1) deficiency causes beriberi and is common in chronic alcoholism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thiamin provides thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP), the cofactor for oxidative decarboxylation enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and for transketolase. Its deficiency causes beriberi with cardiac and peripheral nerve dysfunction and is especially likely in chronic alcoholism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Riboflavin gives FMN/FAD; deficiency is linked to impaired iron absorption and possible normocytic anemia, not beriberi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Niacin gives NAD+/NADP+; its deficiency causes pellagra, not high-output cardiac failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyridoxine gives PLP; deficiency causes convulsions and microcytic anemia, and its cofactor is not used by transketolase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biotin supports carboxylation reactions; deficiency causes dermatitis and metabolic acidosis, not beriberi.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who eats an extremely limited diet with almost no fruits or vegetables presents with bleeding, swollen gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, and a poorly healing surgical wound. The deficient vitamin acts as a coenzyme for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase. Impaired activity of these enzymes most directly explains his findings through defective synthesis of which molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-linked collagen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serotonin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nicotinamide for NAD+

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methionine

explanation.summary: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) impairs collagen hydroxylation and cross-linking.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin C is a coenzyme for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which hydroxylate proline and lysine residues so collagen can cross-link and form stable, mature protein. Without it, collagen is weak, producing the bleeding gums, pinpoint hemorrhages, and poor wound healing of scurvy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heme synthesis begins with ALA synthase using PLP and glycine, and is not the target of prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serotonin synthesis requires BH4 and PLP, not vitamin C-dependent collagen hydroxylases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nicotinamide for NAD+ derives from tryptophan catabolism, unrelated to collagen hydroxylation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methionine is regenerated by methionine synthase using B12 and folate, not by collagen hydroxylases.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has been taking more than 2 grams per day of a vitamin supplement for premenstrual symptoms for several months, roughly 20 times the tolerable upper intake level. She develops numbness beginning in the feet, then loss of sensation in the hands, and eventually difficulty walking. Symptoms resolve after she stops the supplement. Excess of which vitamin best explains this toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin B3 (niacin)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B1 (thiamin)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid)

explanation.summary: Excess vitamin B6 causes a dose-dependent peripheral sensory neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B6 is one of the two water-soluble vitamins (with B3) that can cause adverse effects in excess. Toxicity was recognized in studies of megadose B6 for premenstrual syndrome, producing sensory neuropathy that starts as numb feet and can progress to inability to walk, reversing after supplements are stopped.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess niacin causes a prostaglandin-mediated flush, not a progressive sensory neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The vitamin C UL is 2000 mg/d and excess does not cause this ascending neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thiamin has no established UL and is considered safe even at high doses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pantothenate has no established RDA and deficiency, not excess, is essentially the only concern, and even that is very rare.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A bodybuilder who consumes several raw egg whites daily for months develops thinning hair, a scaly dry rash, and fatigue. His diet is otherwise adequate. A protein in the raw egg white tightly binds a vitamin required by carboxylase enzymes. Which vitamin is most likely deficient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin B7 (biotin)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B9 (folate)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)

explanation.summary: Avidin in raw egg white binds biotin and can cause biotin deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Biotin is the cofactor for carboxylase enzymes such as pyruvate carboxylase. Raw eggs contain avidin, which tightly binds biotin; regular consumption of raw eggs in high quantities can deplete biotin, causing thinning hair and scaly, dry skin. Heat denatures avidin, so cooked eggs are not a concern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Riboflavin is not bound by avidin and its deficiency affects iron absorption and can cause anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia, and folate is not bound by avidin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and neurologic disease, unrelated to raw egg intake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyridoxine is not bound by avidin; its deficiency causes convulsions and microcytic anemia.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old vegan presents with fatigue, macrocytic anemia, and paresthesias. Serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) is markedly elevated. The elevated MMA reflects reduced activity of an enzyme that normally uses this vitamin as a coenzyme. Which enzyme is impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cystathionine beta-synthase

choices.label: D
choices.text: ALA synthase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transketolase

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 is a coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so deficiency raises MMA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 serves as a coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a role distinct from its interdependence with folate at methionine synthase. When this function is impaired, methylmalonic acid accumulates, which is why elevated serum MMA is indicative of B12 deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin, not B12, and its impairment does not elevate MMA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cystathionine beta-synthase is PLP-dependent and its defect causes homocystinuria, not elevated MMA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ALA synthase uses PLP for heme synthesis and is unrelated to MMA accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transketolase uses TPP in the pentose phosphate pathway and does not affect MMA.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is started on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis. His physician co-prescribes vitamin B6 supplementation. Prolonged isoniazid therapy depletes vitamin B6, which is required to synthesize niacin. Without supplementation, the patient would be at greatest risk of developing which condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pellagra

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beriberi

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scurvy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrocytic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Niacin flush reaction

explanation.summary: Isoniazid depletes B6, reducing niacin synthesis and risking pellagra.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-term isoniazid use depletes vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) stores, which are required to synthesize niacin from tryptophan. Reduced niacin availability can culminate in pellagra, which is why patients on isoniazid receive supplemental vitamin B6.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beriberi results from thiamin (B1) deficiency, which isoniazid does not cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency, unrelated to B6 depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrocytic anemia reflects folate or B12 deficiency, not B6 depletion from isoniazid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The niacin flush is a toxicity of excess niacin, the opposite of the deficiency risk here.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A first-year medical student is reviewing which vitamin-derived cofactor is shared by pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase in the reactions of glucose metabolism. Which cofactor correctly completes this assignment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coenzyme A (from B5)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thiamin pyrophosphate (from B1)

choices.label: C
choices.text: FAD (from B2)

choices.label: D
choices.text: NAD+ (from B3)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Biotin (from B7)

explanation.summary: Thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP) is the cofactor shared by these three enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thiamin pyrophosphate (TPP), derived from vitamin B1, is required by pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (oxidative decarboxylation in the TCA cycle) and by transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CoA (from B5) is used in the TCA cycle by enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase but not by transketolase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FAD (from B2) participates in the TCA/electron transport chain (e.g., complex II), not transketolase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NAD+ (from B3) is used broadly in glycolysis and TCA dehydrogenases but is not the transketolase cofactor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biotin (from B7) supports carboxylation in gluconeogenesis (pyruvate carboxylase), not these three enzymes.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A neonate with classic phenylketonuria is being studied. The defective enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine and requires a specific cofactor that is also needed by tyrosine hydroxylase, tryptophan hydroxylase, and nitric oxide synthase. Unlike the B vitamins, this cofactor is a derivative of GTP. Which cofactor is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tetrahydrofolate (FH4)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cobalamin (B12)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Coenzyme A (CoA)

explanation.summary: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is the GTP-derived cofactor for the aromatic hydroxylases and NO synthase.
explanation.whyCorrect: BH4 is a derivative of GTP required by phenylalanine hydroxylase (dysfunctional in classic PKU), tyrosine hydroxylase, and tryptophan hydroxylase, feeding catecholamine and serotonin synthesis. It is also required by nitric oxide synthase to make NO from arginine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PLP (from B6) is used by aminotransferases and decarboxylases, and downstream dopa decarboxylase, but not by phenylalanine hydroxylase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FH4 donates one-carbon units for methionine synthesis and is not the hydroxylase cofactor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cobalamin serves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, not the aromatic hydroxylases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CoA is used in energy-yielding acyl transfer reactions, unrelated to amino acid hydroxylation.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man takes a 1,000 mg dose of niacin for hyperlipidemia. About 20 minutes later he develops red, warm, itchy skin over his face and upper body, which resolves within about an hour. The tolerable upper intake level for niacin is only 35 mg/day, the lowest of the water-soluble vitamins. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prostaglandin release causing cutaneous vasodilation

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation from a true allergy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Accumulation of methylmalonic acid in the skin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired collagen cross-linking in dermal vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral sensory neuropathy from cofactor toxicity

explanation.summary: The niacin flush is a harmless prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous vasodilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exceeding the niacin UL commonly causes a flush reaction with red, warm, itchy skin. Niacin in the bloodstream prompts release of prostaglandins, leading to dilation of skin blood vessels and increased blood flow. It is harmless and temporary, typically subsiding within 1-2 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The flush is a prostaglandin-mediated response, not an IgE-mediated allergic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methylmalonic acid accumulates in B12 deficiency and does not cause cutaneous flushing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective collagen cross-linking is the mechanism of scurvy, not the niacin flush.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sensory neuropathy is a feature of vitamin B6 toxicity, not the transient niacin flush.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A nutrition scientist is assessing the adequacy of nutrient intake in a large group of healthy adults. She compares the group's observed intake with the average daily level estimated to meet the requirement of 50% of healthy individuals in the defined population, a value that also serves as the foundational reference point for deriving the RDA. Which dietary reference intake value is she using?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adequate Intake (AI)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dietary Reference Intake (DRI)

explanation.summary: The EAR is the intake meeting the requirement of 50% of healthy individuals and is the basis for the RDA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Estimated Average Requirement is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirements of half of the healthy individuals in a defined population. It is usually used to assess the nutrient intakes of groups of people and to plan nutritionally adequate diets for them, and it is the foundational reference point for determining the RDA. On the DRI curve, the EAR is the intake at which the risk of inadequacy is 50%.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The RDA is derived from the EAR and covers nearly all (97-98%) individuals in a cohort, not 50%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The AI is an observational or experimental approximation set only when evidence is lacking to calculate an EAR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The UL is the maximum daily intake unlikely to cause adverse effects, a safety ceiling rather than a requirement estimate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DRI is the collective term for the whole set of reference values, not the specific 50% value.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man purchases high-dose B-complex tablets, believing the vitamins themselves will be 'burned' for energy during his workouts. Which of the following best describes how the water soluble B vitamins actually contribute to energy metabolism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are oxidized directly to yield ATP when broken down

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are stored in adipose tissue and mobilized during exercise

choices.label: C
choices.text: They provide carbon skeletons that enter the TCA cycle as fuel

choices.label: D
choices.text: They act as hormones that stimulate appetite and food intake

choices.label: E
choices.text: They act as coenzymes for enzymes that capture energy from food

explanation.summary: Water soluble vitamins are coenzymes; they do not themselves yield usable energy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The water soluble vitamins help the body maximize the nutrient value of dietary carbohydrates, fats, and proteins by helping synthesize important molecules, break down food to capture energy as ATP, or assist certain pathways. They do not in and of themselves yield usable energy when broken down. The B vitamins and vitamin C accomplish this by acting as coenzymes, whose active forms participate in anabolic, catabolic, and intermediate reactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B vitamins are not metabolized to directly produce energy; they enable enzymes that do so.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These vitamins are water soluble and act as coenzymes, not as a stored fuel reserve.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They do not serve as fuel substrates for the TCA cycle; they are cofactors for TCA enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B vitamins are enzyme helpers, not hormones regulating appetite.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A public health officer reviews national regulations requiring fortification of breads and cereals, a practice credited with drastically reducing certain vitamin deficiencies. In addition to the minerals iron and calcium, grain products are most commonly fortified with which combination of vitamins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B1, B2, and B3

choices.label: B
choices.text: B6, B9, and B12

choices.label: C
choices.text: B5, B7, and C

choices.label: D
choices.text: B2, B6, and B7

choices.label: E
choices.text: B9, B12, and C

explanation.summary: Grain products are most commonly fortified with vitamins B1, B2, and B3 plus iron and calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diets built on refined, unenriched grains leave patients susceptible to vitamin B deficiencies. Fortifying grain products such as breads and cereals with vitamin B has drastically reduced deficiency, and these products are most commonly fortified with vitamins B1, B2, and B3 along with minerals such as iron and calcium, under regulations set by the Food and Drug Administration in the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.B: B6, B9, and B12 are not the vitamins most commonly added to grain products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pantothenate is already widely available in foods, and biotin and vitamin C are not the standard grain fortificants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin is a common fortificant, but B6 and B7 are not part of the standard trio.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate, B12, and vitamin C are not the combination most commonly used for grain fortification.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with a chronic liver condition has serum ALT and AST measured. These enzymes catalyze the 'swap' of an amino group from an amino acid donor with a carbonyl group on an alpha-keto acid, a reaction central to amino acid catabolism and the transformation and transportation of nitrogen. Which vitamin-derived cofactor do these enzymes require?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thiamin pyrophosphate (from B1)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flavin adenine dinucleotide (from B2)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coenzyme A (from B5)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (from B6)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Biotin (from B7)

explanation.summary: Aminotransferases such as ALT and AST are PLP-dependent enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyridoxal phosphate, derived from vitamin B6, is the cofactor for aminotransferase (transaminase) reactions in which an amino functional group from an amino acid donor is swapped with a carbonyl group on an alpha-keto acid. ALT and AST are the predominant examples, and these PLP-dependent reactions are critical in amino acid catabolism and nitrogen transport.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TPP serves oxidative decarboxylation enzymes and transketolase, not aminotransferases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FAD serves enzymes such as succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II), not transamination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CoA participates in acyl transfer in the TCA cycle, not amino group transfer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biotin is used for carboxylation reactions that add CO2 to a substrate.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A researcher studies the two-step conversion of tryptophan to serotonin, a neurotransmitter that regulates sleep, mood, and appetite in the brain and mediates platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction when formed in platelets. The first step is catalyzed by tryptophan hydroxylase and the second by dopa decarboxylase. Which pair of cofactors is required for this pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: TPP and NAD+

choices.label: B
choices.text: BH4 and PLP

choices.label: C
choices.text: FH4 and cobalamin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Biotin and CoA

choices.label: E
choices.text: BH4 and FAD

explanation.summary: Serotonin synthesis requires both BH4 (tryptophan hydroxylase) and PLP (dopa decarboxylase).
explanation.whyCorrect: Tryptophan hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) to hydroxylate tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan, and dopa decarboxylase then requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) to decarboxylate 5-hydroxytryptophan, releasing CO2, to form serotonin. This illustrates how many pathways rely on multiple nutrient factors: the serotonin pathway needs both BH4 and PLP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TPP and NAD+ serve glucose metabolism enzymes such as PDH, not the serotonin pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FH4 and cobalamin cooperate at methionine synthase, not in tryptophan hydroxylation or decarboxylation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biotin and CoA are used in carboxylation and acyl transfer, not serotonin synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BH4 is correct for the hydroxylase, but the decarboxylase requires PLP, not FAD.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A dietitian explains that one B vitamin is so widely available in foods that its name derives from a word meaning 'everywhere,' and that deficiency in humans has essentially only been considered in hypothetical situations such as mouse models. No RDA has been established for it, in part because no indicators have been found that specifically and sensitively reflect its deficiency in humans. Which vitamin is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin B1 (thiamin)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin B5 (pantothenate)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B7 (biotin)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B9 (folate)

explanation.summary: Pantothenate ('pantos' = everywhere) deficiency is among the rarest, and no RDA exists for it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of its ready availability in various foodstuffs, vitamin B5 (pantothenate) deficiency is one of the rarest of all B-vitamin deficiencies, with only hypothetical situations such as mouse models available for consideration. Although its constituent coenzyme A is required in about 100 different reactions in mammalian cells, no RDA has been established, partly because no specific and sensitive indicators of deficiency have been found in humans.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thiamin has a defined RDA (1.4 mg/day is cited) and a well-known deficiency, beriberi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biotin deficiency is rare but does occur, for example with raw egg consumption or biotinidase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin deficiency is recognized clinically and can be measured with erythrocyte glutathione reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate deficiency is well characterized, causing macrocytic anemia and birth defects.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old healthy woman reads that her daily intake of a vitamin is exactly at the RDA for her age and sex cohort and worries that she is consuming only the bare minimum required. Which of the following statements about the RDA is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It meets the requirement of 50% of individuals, so half the people at this intake are inadequate

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the maximum intake unlikely to cause adverse effects, so exceeding it is hazardous

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is set from observation of healthy groups when evidence is lacking to calculate a requirement

choices.label: D
choices.text: It meets the needs of 97-98% of individuals in the cohort and is not a minimal requirement

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the intake at which the risk of adverse effects begins to increase with further intake

explanation.summary: The RDA covers 97-98% of a cohort and should not be interpreted as the minimal requirement.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Recommended Dietary Allowance is the average daily intake sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97-98%) individuals within a select age or sex cohort, and it is often used to plan nutritionally adequate diets for individuals. At the RDA the risk of inadequacy is only about 2-3%. The RDA should not be interpreted as the minimal requirement for healthy individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 50% value is the EAR, not the RDA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The maximum intake unlikely to cause adverse effects is the UL, not the RDA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A value set from observation when an EAR cannot be calculated is the AI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Risk of adverse effects increases above the UL, not above the RDA.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is admitted with beriberi heart disease and started on intravenous thiamin at 150 mg/day, roughly 100 times the RDA of 1.4 mg/day. A medical student asks whether this dose exceeds the tolerable upper intake level and endangers the patient. Which response is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The dose exceeds the UL of 35 mg/day and should be reduced to avoid a flush reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: The dose exceeds the UL of 100 mg/day and risks a peripheral sensory neuropathy

choices.label: C
choices.text: No UL exists for thiamin because high intakes have not caused adverse effects

choices.label: D
choices.text: The dose is acceptable only because intravenous administration bypasses the oral UL

choices.label: E
choices.text: The dose should be limited to the UL of 2000 mg/day used for water soluble vitamins

explanation.summary: Thiamin has no established UL and is considered safe even at high doses.
explanation.whyCorrect: There is no concern with 150 mg/day because of the water soluble nature of thiamin. As with many water soluble members of the vitamin B series, there is no established Tolerable Upper Intake Level for thiamin (vitamin B1) because there have been no reports of adverse effects from high intakes. Thiamin is considered safe even at high doses, and the cardiac and peripheral nerve dysfunction of beriberi usually responds to thiamin replacement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 35 mg/day is the UL for niacin, the lowest of the water soluble vitamins, and the flush is a niacin reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 100 mg/day is the UL for vitamin B6, whose excess causes sensory neuropathy; thiamin has no UL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The safety of the dose reflects the absence of any UL for thiamin, not the route of administration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 2000 mg/day is the UL for vitamin C specifically, not a generic ceiling for water soluble vitamins.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a restricted diet has mild normocytic anemia and sub-optimal absorption of dietary iron. To assess her vitamin status, the laboratory measures the activity of glutathione reductase isolated from her erythrocytes. Which vitamin is being evaluated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin B1 (thiamin)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin B3 (niacin)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)

explanation.summary: Riboflavin status is measured with erythrocyte glutathione reductase; deficiency impairs iron absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B2 is required for the FAD and FMN coenzymes, and its deficiency causes sub-optimal dietary iron absorption and possibly a normocytic anemia. Riboflavin status can be measured in a patient using isolated glutathione reductase from erythrocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thiamin status was historically assessed by transketolase activity, an antiquated method, not glutathione reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Niacin deficiency produces pellagra and is not assessed by erythrocyte glutathione reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyridoxine deficiency causes microcytic anemia and convulsions; it is not assessed with this assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin C promotes iron absorption via duodenal cytochrome B, but its status is not measured with glutathione reductase.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with a diet severely lacking in vitamin B6 becomes lightheaded and weak after an overnight fast, and his blood glucose is low. Impaired activity of which of the following enzymes best explains his difficulty maintaining blood glucose during fasting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycogen phosphorylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transketolase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase

explanation.summary: PLP is a required cofactor of hepatic glycogen phosphorylase, which provides glucose during fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyridoxal phosphate is a required cofactor of glycogen phosphorylase in the liver, the enzyme that provides glucose during times of fasting. With vitamin B6 deficiency, this activity is impaired and the ability to maintain blood glucose during a fast is compromised.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin; its impairment causes fasting hypoglycemia in biotin, not B6, deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase requires NADP+, a B3 derivative, and acts in the pentose phosphate pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transketolase requires TPP and functions in the pentose phosphate pathway, not glucose release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires TPP, CoA, FAD, and NAD+ and oxidizes pyruvate rather than releasing glucose.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a prolonged dietary deficiency of vitamin B6 is found to have a microcytic anemia. Which of the following reactions is most directly impaired, accounting for her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduction of Fe3+ to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B

choices.label: B
choices.text: ATP-dependent carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methylation of homocysteine to form methionine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA into ALA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydroxylation of lysine residues in collagen

explanation.summary: PLP is required by ALA synthase, the first step of heme synthesis, so B6 deficiency causes microcytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within the mitochondria, aminolevulinic acid synthase converts glycine and succinyl-CoA into aminolevulinic acid (ALA) in the first step of heme synthesis, and this enzyme requires PLP. Heme is used to form hemoglobin within erythrocytes, myoglobin within tissues, and the prosthetic group of cytochrome P450 enzymes. Vitamin B6 deficiency therefore produces a microcytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reduction of Fe3+ to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B depends on vitamin C, not B6.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate carboxylation is biotin dependent and relates to gluconeogenesis, not heme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methionine synthase uses B12 and folate; its impairment causes macrocytic, not microcytic, anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysyl hydroxylase requires vitamin C and affects collagen, not heme synthesis.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant with severe vitamin B6 deficiency develops recurrent convulsions that resolve after pyridoxine administration. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of the seizures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired transamination of alanine to pyruvate reduces gluconeogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of glycogen phosphorylase activity causes fasting hypoglycemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased ALA synthase activity reduces heme available to neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced hydroxylation of phenylalanine to tyrosine in the brain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased decarboxylation of substrates for neurotransmitter synthesis

explanation.summary: B6 deficiency impairs PLP-dependent decarboxylation needed to form neurotransmitters, causing convulsions.
explanation.whyCorrect: PLP is required for the formation of multiple neurotransmitters. Convulsions may result from a decreased ability to decarboxylate (remove a carboxylic acid as CO2) substrates for neurotransmitter synthesis, such as the PLP-dependent dopa decarboxylase step that converts dopa to dopamine and 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transamination is PLP dependent, but the convulsions are attributed to neurotransmitter formation, not gluconeogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogen phosphorylase is PLP dependent and affects fasting glucose, but this is not the stated mechanism of the seizures.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ALA synthase impairment explains the microcytic anemia of B6 deficiency, not convulsions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires BH4, not PLP, so it is not affected by B6 deficiency.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with a rare biotin deficiency presents with hypotonia, fatigue, and fasting hypoglycemia. Laboratory studies show lactic acidosis. Impaired activity of which enzyme best explains the combination of hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glycogen phosphorylase

explanation.summary: Biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase drives gluconeogenesis; its loss causes hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Biotin is required for carboxylation reactions, the most important of which is in gluconeogenesis, where pyruvate carboxylase adds CO2 to pyruvate using ATP to form oxaloacetate. Biotin deficiency produces hypotonia and fatigue due to fasting hypoglycemia from compromised gluconeogenesis, and lactic acidosis due to an inability to use pyruvate in gluconeogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate dehydrogenase uses TPP, CoA, FAD, and NAD+, not biotin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase is biotin dependent, but its inhibition causes an organic acidemia from propionic acid, not fasting hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses vitamin B12 and its impairment raises methylmalonic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycogen phosphorylase requires PLP and is not affected by biotin deficiency.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has thinning hair, a scaly dry rash, hypotonia, and metabolic acidosis despite a diet containing adequate biotin. Enzyme testing reveals deficiency of the enzyme that liberates biotin from proteins, recycling it from both dietary and bodily sources. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoidance of raw egg whites

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-dose niacin supplementation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B7 supplementation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravenous thiamin replacement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C with iron supplementation

explanation.summary: Biotinidase deficiency causes biotin deficiency and is treated with vitamin B7 supplementation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Biotinidase recycles biotin by liberating it from proteins, functioning on both dietary and bodily sources. Biotinidase deficiency therefore causes a biotin deficiency, with thinning hair, scaly dry skin, hypotonia, neurological issues, and metabolic acidosis. The condition is typically treated with vitamin B7 (biotin) supplementation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Avidin in raw eggs can deplete biotin, but this infant's problem is failure to recycle biotin, not avidin binding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Niacin treats pellagra and does not correct a biotin recycling defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thiamin is used for beriberi and does not address biotin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin C with iron improves iron absorption and is unrelated to biotinidase deficiency.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with iron deficiency anemia is prescribed an iron supplement that also contains vitamin C and is advised to take it with citrus juice, since eating vitamin C together with iron-containing foods can double or even triple iron absorption. Which mechanism best explains this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin C chelates Fe3+ and carries it across the enterocyte membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin C hydroxylates transferrin to increase its iron-binding capacity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin C triggers prostaglandin release that increases intestinal blood flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin C is a coenzyme for duodenal cytochrome B, reducing Fe3+ to Fe2+

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C raises erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity to spare iron

explanation.summary: Vitamin C enables duodenal cytochrome B to reduce Fe3+ to the absorbable Fe2+ form.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin C is required for absorption of dietary iron as a coenzyme for duodenal cytochrome B, which converts Fe3+ to Fe2+, because only the +2 form is absorbed. This is why eating vitamin C-containing foods with iron-containing foods at the same meal can double or triple iron absorption and why many iron supplements contain vitamin C.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin C acts as a coenzyme for a reducing enzyme, not as a carrier that chelates and transports Fe3+.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin C hydroxylates proline and lysine in collagen, not transferrin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation is the mechanism of the niacin flush, not iron absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutathione reductase activity reflects riboflavin status and does not mediate iron uptake.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with riboflavin deficiency has reduced availability of FAD. Which of the following enzymes, which functions both in the TCA cycle and as Complex II of the electron transport chain, is most directly affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isocitrate dehydrogenase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Succinate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Malate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyruvate carboxylase

explanation.summary: Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) is the FAD-dependent enzyme shared by the TCA cycle and ETC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Riboflavin provides FMN and FAD. Among the enzymes of glucose metabolism, FAD is required by Complex II of the electron transport chain, which is the same enzyme as succinate dehydrogenase in the TCA cycle, as well as by pyruvate dehydrogenase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a TCA enzyme that uses NAD+ (from niacin), not FAD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malate dehydrogenase is a TCA enzyme that uses NAD+, not FAD, and is not part of the ETC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase is a glycolytic NAD+-dependent enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent gluconeogenic enzyme.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with pellagra has reduced availability of NAD+. Which of the following enzymes of glucose metabolism is most directly dependent on a niacin-derived coenzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transketolase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Succinate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isocitrate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glycogen phosphorylase

explanation.summary: NAD+ (from niacin) is required by isocitrate dehydrogenase and other dehydrogenases of glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Niacin forms NAD+ and NADP+, which are required in glycolysis and the TCA cycle by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase. Of the options listed, only isocitrate dehydrogenase uses the niacin-derived coenzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway requires TPP from thiamin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) requires FAD from riboflavin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin for carboxylation in gluconeogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycogen phosphorylase requires PLP from vitamin B6.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has impaired availability of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). In addition to elevated phenylalanine, he has decreased production of dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. Reduced activity of which enzyme most directly accounts for the decreased catecholamine synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dopa decarboxylase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tyrosine hydroxylase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tryptophan hydroxylase

explanation.summary: BH4 is required by tyrosine hydroxylase, the step leading toward dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: BH4 is required by phenylalanine hydroxylase to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine and by tyrosine hydroxylase in the subsequent step that ultimately leads to dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. Dopamine regulates normal motor activity, while norepinephrine and epinephrine regulate carbohydrate and lipid metabolism and increase blood pressure and cardiac output, so loss of tyrosine hydroxylase activity reduces all three catecholamines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dopa decarboxylase requires PLP, not BH4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase uses O2, Cu2+, and vitamin C to make norepinephrine and is not BH4 dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase uses S-adenosylmethionine to convert norepinephrine to epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tryptophan hydroxylase is BH4 dependent but serves serotonin synthesis, not catecholamines.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A vascular biologist studies an enzyme that produces the membrane-permeable gas nitric oxide, which activates cytosolic guanylate cyclase to generate cGMP for cell signaling. The enzyme consumes NADPH and O2 and requires tetrahydrobiopterin. Which amino acid serves as its substrate, and what is the co-product formed with nitric oxide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tyrosine; dopa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tryptophan; 5-hydroxytryptophan

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycine; aminolevulinic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homocysteine; cystathionine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arginine; citrulline

explanation.summary: Nitric oxide synthase converts arginine to citrulline plus NO in a BH4-dependent step.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitric oxide synthesis requires BH4 and uses the amino acid arginine as substrate. Nitric oxide synthase, with NADPH and O2, converts arginine to citrulline plus NO, generating NADP+ and water. NO then activates cytosolic guanylate cyclase for cGMP generation and cell signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tyrosine to dopa is the BH4-dependent tyrosine hydroxylase reaction, not NO synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan is the BH4-dependent tryptophan hydroxylase reaction toward serotonin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycine to aminolevulinic acid is the PLP-dependent first step of heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homocysteine to cystathionine is the PLP-dependent cystathionine beta-synthase step.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a metastatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes high levels of serotonin develops chronic diarrhea, a scaly hyperpigmented rash on sun-exposed skin, and confusion. Which mechanism best explains his vitamin deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Augmented tryptophan catabolism to serotonin limits nicotinamide synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A defective neutral amino acid transporter causes urinary tryptophan loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of vitamin B6 stores prevents conversion of tryptophan to niacin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binding of niacin by a heat-labile protein in the gut prevents its absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostaglandin release accelerates renal excretion of NAD+ precursors

explanation.summary: Carcinoid syndrome diverts tryptophan into serotonin, reducing niacin availability and causing pellagra.
explanation.whyCorrect: In carcinoid syndrome, tryptophan catabolism is augmented within a select type of cancer cell that secretes high levels of serotonin, and serotonin synthesis requires tryptophan. Because tryptophan can otherwise be used to contribute nicotinamide for NAD+ synthesis, a decrement in available tryptophan can produce pellagra with its dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective neutral amino acid transporter with urinary tryptophan loss is Hartnup disease, not a serotonin-secreting tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin B6 depletion is the mechanism of pellagra in prolonged isoniazid therapy, not carcinoid syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Avidin in raw egg white binds biotin, not niacin, and is unrelated to this tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandin release underlies the niacin flush reaction and does not cause niacin loss.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with prolonged biotin deficiency presents with metabolic acidosis. Analysis reveals accumulation of propionic acid derived from amino acid catabolism, consistent with an organic acidemia. Inhibition of which enzyme is responsible for this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cystathionine beta-synthase

explanation.summary: Biotin deficiency inhibits propionyl-CoA carboxylase, causing propionic acid accumulation (organic acidemia).
explanation.whyCorrect: Biotin deficiency can cause metabolic acidosis due to accumulation of organic acids known as organic acidemias. These result from accumulation of select metabolites such as propionic acid from amino acid catabolism due to inhibited propionyl-CoA carboxylase, a biotin-dependent carboxylase. This is the same pathway that requires vitamin B12 downstream to prevent methylmalonic acid accumulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is B12 dependent; its impairment causes methylmalonic acid, not propionic acid, to accumulate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyruvate carboxylase is biotin dependent, but its loss causes fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis rather than propionic acidemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase requires TPP, CoA, FAD, and NAD+, not biotin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cystathionine beta-synthase is PLP dependent and its defect causes homocystinuria.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man living alone on a diet devoid of fruits and vegetables for many months has bleeding gums, pinpoint skin hemorrhages, rough brown scaly skin, painful softened ends of the long bones, and loose teeth. Without treatment, which of the following is the most likely cause of sudden death in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Massive bleeding into the joints and body cavities

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-output cardiac failure from cardiomyopathy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progressive coma from central nervous system involvement

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactic acidosis from impaired gluconeogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypoglycemic coma from failed hepatic glycogenolysis

explanation.summary: Advanced scurvy can cause sudden death from massive bleeding into joints and body cavities.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has scurvy from vitamin C deficiency. Initial signs relate to loss of structural integrity in blood vessels, with bleeding gums and pinpoint hemorrhages; later, muscles including the heart may degenerate, wounds fail to heal, bone rebuilding falters so the ends of the long bones soften and become painful, and teeth loosen. Sudden death is likely, perhaps because of massive bleeding into the joints and body cavities.

whyWrongByChoice.B: High-output cardiac failure from cardiomyopathy is the picture of wet beriberi (thiamin deficiency).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Progression to a comatose state and death describes untreated pellagra (niacin deficiency).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactic acidosis from impaired gluconeogenesis is a feature of biotin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure of glycogen phosphorylase reflects vitamin B6 deficiency, not scurvy.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with homocystinuria has markedly elevated homocysteine. Evaluation localizes the defect to the enzyme of the transsulfuration pathway that converts homocysteine to cystathionine on the way to cysteine. Which vitamin-derived cofactor does this enzyme require?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methylcobalamin (from B12)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methyl-tetrahydrofolate (from B9)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thiamin pyrophosphate (from B1)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tetrahydrobiopterin (from GTP)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (from B6)

explanation.summary: Cystathionine beta-synthase, which converts homocysteine to cystathionine, is PLP dependent.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the transsulfuration pathway, homocysteine is converted to cystathionine by cystathionine beta-synthase, which is PLP dependent, and cystathionine is then converted to cysteine, which feeds back to inhibit the synthase. A defect at this step raises homocysteine, as seen in homocystinuria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methylcobalamin serves methionine synthase, which remethylates homocysteine to methionine, not the transsulfuration step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methyl-FH4 donates the one-carbon unit to B12 for methionine synthase, not to cystathionine beta-synthase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TPP serves oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase reactions, not sulfur amino acid metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BH4 serves the aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and nitric oxide synthase, not cystathionine beta-synthase.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with vitamin B12 deficiency has elevated serum methylmalonic acid. Several amino acids are catabolized through the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase pathway so that their carbon skeletons are fed into the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA. Which of the following amino acids is catabolized in this manner?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leucine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phenylalanine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tryptophan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Isoleucine

explanation.summary: Valine, isoleucine, threonine, and methionine converge on the B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 is a coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which is why elevated methylmalonic acid indicates B12 deficiency. A variety of substrates converge to use this pathway so that upon catabolism their carbon skeletons are fed into the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA; the amino acids catabolized in this manner are valine, isoleucine, threonine, and methionine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leucine is a branched chain amino acid but is not among the amino acids listed as entering via succinyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine by a BH4-dependent enzyme and is not catabolized via methylmalonyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tryptophan is oxidized via acetyl-CoA or used for nicotinamide and serotonin, not via methylmalonyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycine condenses with succinyl-CoA in heme synthesis; it is not catabolized through methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism (1 of 3)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis is evaluated for poor weight gain and greasy, foul-smelling stools. His parents report he has recently had trouble seeing in dim light. Laboratory testing confirms pancreatic insufficiency with low fecal elastase. Which of the following best explains why this child is at risk for vitamin A deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thick mucus blocks pancreatic ducts, reducing lipase delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess renal excretion of the water-soluble vitamin depletes body stores

choices.label: C
choices.text: A congenital defect in hepatic 25-hydroxylase prevents activation of the vitamin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gut bacteria that synthesize the vitamin are eradicated by chronic antibiotic use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoantibodies destroy the intestinal receptor required for active transport of the vitamin

explanation.summary: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) require normal fat digestion; conditions that impair lipid absorption cause their deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus blocks pancreatic secretory ducts and reduces lipase release into the small intestine, adversely impacting fat absorption. Because fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed with lipids and incorporated into chylomicrons formed during fat digestion, any pathology that impairs lipid absorption traps these vitamins in the digestive tract and causes deficiency. Night blindness is an early indicator of vitamin A deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin A is fat-soluble, not water-soluble, and is stored in liver and adipose rather than being lost readily in urine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 25-hydroxylase acts on vitamin D3, not vitamin A, and this is not the mechanism of malabsorption in cystic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of vitamin K-producing gut bacteria affects vitamin K, not vitamin A, and is not the cause here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed passively with dietary lipids, not through a specific autoantibody-targeted active transporter.

questions.topicName: Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with known chronic pancreatic disease comes to the clinic complaining of difficulty seeing while driving home at night. Physical exam of the anterior eye later shows a dry, hardened cornea and small foamy patches on the conjunctiva. Which form of vitamin A most directly explains his night vision problem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Retinal, a component of rhodopsin needed for visual pigment regeneration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Retinoic acid, which activates nuclear receptors to regulate keratin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retinol bound to its transport protein for storage in the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-carotene, the plant carotenoid precursor of vitamin A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Calcitriol, the active hormonal derivative that governs gene expression

explanation.summary: Night blindness in vitamin A deficiency results from insufficient retinal for regeneration of visual pigment in the retina.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retinal is the component of rhodopsin, the light-sensing biological pigment in cells at the back of the eye. Night blindness occurs when insufficient retinal is present for visual pigment regeneration, and it is an early indicator of vitamin A deficiency. His dry hardened cornea (corneal xerosis) and conjunctival Bitot's spots reflect progression of the same deficiency (xerophthalmia).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Retinoic acid acts as a hormone regulating gene expression and keratin production but is not the light-sensing molecule of the retina.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Retinol is the major transport and storage form of vitamin A, not the pigment that directly senses light.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-carotene is the inactive plant precursor cleaved into vitamin A; it is not itself the visual pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcitriol is the active form of vitamin D, unrelated to visual pigment function.

questions.topicName: Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)

questions.stem: A dermatologist plans to prescribe isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) for a 19-year-old woman with severe cystic acne. Before starting therapy she is enrolled in a program requiring two negative pregnancy tests and adherence to a strict contraception regimen. Which property of this retinoid best justifies these precautions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is teratogenic because it modulates transcription factors that affect fetal development

choices.label: B
choices.text: It causes irreversible maternal night blindness during pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: It precipitates as calcium oxalate and forms fetal kidney stones

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits epoxide reductase and causes fetal hemorrhage

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is rapidly converted from beta-carotene and accumulates to toxic levels in the fetus

explanation.summary: Excess vitamin A is a well-known teratogen and is of great concern in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retinoic acid acts as a hormone that regulates cell differentiation and embryonic development by modulating transcription. Excess vitamin A poses a teratogenic risk to the developing fetus and increases the risk of birth defects, which is why isotretinoin (Accutane) requires strict contraception and negative pregnancy tests before prescription.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Night blindness is a sign of vitamin A deficiency, not toxicity, and is not the reason for contraception requirements.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium oxalate stones are a feature of vitamin D toxicity, not retinoid teratogenicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epoxide reductase inhibition describes warfarin's effect on vitamin K, not isotretinoin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-carotene conversion is too slow to cause toxicity and describes a mechanism protecting against, not causing, vitamin A toxicity.

questions.topicName: Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). She is started on all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) and achieves complete remission. Which mechanism best explains the therapeutic effect of ATRA in this leukemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It drives differentiation of the leukemic cells into mature granulocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly triggers apoptosis by cross-linking leukemic cell DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits CYP26 enzymes to prevent catabolism of the leukemic cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It chelates calcium needed for leukemic cell proliferation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It blocks 1-alpha-hydroxylase, starving the tumor of active vitamin D

explanation.summary: ATRA treats APL by promoting differentiation of the leukemic cells rather than killing them directly.
explanation.whyCorrect: All-trans-retinoic acid is first-line therapy for acute promyelocytic leukemia. Its mechanism is to drive differentiation of the leukemic cells into nondividing mature granulocytes/macrophages, and it has proven extremely effective, with about 90% of patients achieving complete remission.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ATRA works by inducing differentiation, not by directly cross-linking DNA to trigger apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP26 inhibition describes retinoic acid metabolism blocking agents (RAMBAs), which raise RA levels; it is not the mechanism of ATRA's action in APL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium chelation (by EDTA/EGTA) relates to preventing coagulation in phlebotomy, not to APL therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1-alpha-hydroxylase acts in vitamin D activation and is unrelated to ATRA's differentiating effect.

questions.topicName: Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)

questions.stem: A 9-month-old exclusively breastfed infant with darkly pigmented skin who lives in a northern city and gets little sun exposure is brought in for delayed motor milestones. Exam shows bowing of the legs, bone tenderness, and delayed closure of the fontanelles. Which vitamin deficiency best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vitamin D

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin E

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin K

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C

explanation.summary: Rickets from vitamin D deficiency causes soft, poorly mineralized bones in children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets, the softening and weakening of bones in children. Features include delayed growth, bowing of the legs, bone pain and tenderness, and delayed closing of the fontanelles due to poor mineralization of newly formed bone. Lack of sunlight, darker skin tones with less UV absorption, and breastfeeding without supplementation are all contributing risk factors present in this infant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and eye/skin changes, not bowed bones and delayed fontanelle closure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin E deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, not a rachitic bone phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding and prolonged coagulation, not bone deformities.
