choices.text: The proportion of the mineral stored in bone

explanation.summary: The 'macro' in macromineral refers only to how much must be consumed, not to importance or size.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrominerals, also called major minerals, are those required in large amounts, whereas trace minerals (microminerals) are required in small quantities. The classification is based purely on the quantity needed in the diet to make up for daily losses through sweat, urine, and feces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The term does not refer to the relative size of the mineral.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrominerals are not classified as more important than trace minerals; the term refers to quantity required.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The body cannot synthesize any minerals, so all must come from the diet.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bone storage is not the basis for the macromineral versus trace mineral distinction.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A medical student learns that 99% of the body's calcium is stored in bone as hydroxyapatite. Approximately what percentage of the body's phosphate is stored in bone?

explanation.summary: Bone stores 99% of body calcium and 86% of body phosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Calcium and phosphate are both major components of bone hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2, and bone acts as a reserve for both minerals. Calcium is stored primarily in bone (99%), as is phosphate (86%); the remainder circulates or serves in ATP, DNA, RNA, and cellular signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Far more than half of body phosphate is in bone; 50% describes the fraction of serum calcium bound to protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This understates the bone phosphate reserve, which is 86%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 99% is the fraction of calcium, not phosphate, stored in bone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphate is not entirely in bone; it is also a component of ATP, DNA, and RNA and circulates in the blood.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department during a panic episode with a respiratory rate of 32/min, perioral tingling, and spasm of the hands. Arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.55. Which of the following best explains her neuromuscular symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extra protons displace calcium from albumin, raising the ionized fraction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fewer protons occupy albumin's negative sites, lowering the ionized fraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased renal filtration of complexed calcium lowers the total calcium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Calcitonin release from parafollicular cells lowers the ionized fraction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impaired PTH secretion from the parathyroid glands lowers the ionized fraction

explanation.summary: Alkalemia lowers ionized calcium because more negative sites on albumin are free to bind calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like ionized calcium, protons bind negative charges on albumin. In alkalemia there are fewer hydrogen ions available to occupy those sites, so the additional free negative sites bind ionized calcium, decreasing the ionized calcium concentration. Because ionized calcium is the metabolically active fraction, the fall produces paresthesia and tetany.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Proton displacement of albumin-bound calcium occurs in acidemia and raises, not lowers, ionized calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The change with pH is in albumin binding, not in renal filtration of the complexed fraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcitonin is stimulated by high blood calcium, not by alkalemia, and is not the mechanism here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PTH secretion depends on magnesium and is stimulated by hypocalcemia; alkalemia does not act through impaired PTH.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has a serum albumin of 2.0 g/dL and a total serum calcium below the reference range. He has no muscle cramps, tetany, or paresthesias. Which of the following best explains the absence of hypocalcemic symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cirrhotic liver releases stored calcium into the blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low albumin increases renal tubular reabsorption of calcium

choices.label: C
choices.text: The complexed fraction expands to replace the protein-bound fraction

choices.label: D
choices.text: A larger percentage of circulating calcium is in the free ionized form

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low albumin stimulates calcitonin, which protects against tetany

explanation.summary: Hypoalbuminemia increases the percentage of free ionized calcium, so a low total calcium may not reflect low active calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: About half of circulating calcium is bound to albumin and is not metabolically active; the ionized free fraction is what matters clinically. When albumin is low there is less protein to bind calcium, so hypoalbuminemia (like acidemia) increases the percentage of calcium that is free and ionized. The total calcium falls with the loss of the bound fraction while the active ionized fraction is relatively preserved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The liver is not a calcium reservoir; bone holds 99% of body calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Albumin has no described effect on renal tubular calcium reabsorption; PTH controls that process.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The complexed fraction is a small 5%-7% pool bound to phosphate or bicarbonate and does not expand to replace bound calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcitonin lowers calcium in response to high blood calcium and would not protect against hypocalcemia.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A physiologist measures calcium in the glomerular filtrate of a healthy subject. In addition to ionized calcium, which of the following fractions of circulating calcium is expected to appear in the filtrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 5%-7% fraction complexed with phosphate or bicarbonate

choices.label: B
choices.text: The roughly half of ECF calcium bound to albumin

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 99% of body calcium held in bone hydroxyapatite

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1% of body calcium held in the intracellular fluid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The calcium released only after osteoclastic resorption

explanation.summary: Complexed calcium is soluble and is filtered and excreted like ionized calcium; protein-bound calcium is not.
explanation.whyCorrect: Circulating calcium exists in three forms: protein-bound, ionized, and complexed. The complexed fraction (5%-7%) is bound to phosphate or bicarbonate in soluble form, so it can be filtered and excreted by the kidney just like the ionic form. Protein-bound calcium, in contrast, is not available for renal filtration.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Albumin-bound calcium is not directly available for metabolic action or for renal filtration and excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bone hydroxyapatite is a storage pool and is not part of the circulating calcium that reaches the glomerulus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracellular calcium is not in the plasma and is not filtered by the glomerulus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcium released by resorption enters the blood in the same ionized or complexed forms; this is not a distinct filterable fraction.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A biochemist studies an ion that, besides forming bone mineral, is a structural component of ATP, DNA, and RNA and mediates oxygen release from red blood cells. Which of the following ions is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Magnesium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zinc

choices.label: D
choices.text: Copper

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phosphate

explanation.summary: Phosphate is a component of ATP, DNA, and RNA and mediates muscle contraction, cell metabolism, and oxygen release from red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although less popular than calcium, phosphate is a vital ion. It mediates cellular activities including muscle contraction, cell metabolism via ATP, and oxygen release from red blood cells, and it is a structural component of ATP, DNA, and RNA as well as of bone hydroxyapatite.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium is a signaling molecule (IP3, calmodulin) and clotting factor but is not a structural component of ATP, DNA, or RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Magnesium stabilizes ATP by coordinating its phosphate groups but is not itself part of the ATP, DNA, or RNA backbone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Zinc is an enzyme cofactor for more than 100 reactions, not a structural component of nucleic acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Copper is a cofactor for enzymes such as lysyl oxidase and cytochrome c oxidase, not a nucleic acid component.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A researcher blocks calcium entry into presynaptic nerve terminals in an isolated neuromuscular preparation. Which of the following processes is most directly impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolysis of ATP to release stored energy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Release of neurotransmitter into the synapse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transfer of electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cross-linking of lysine residues in collagen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conversion of superoxide to hydrogen peroxide

explanation.summary: Calcium is required for neurotransmitter release in cell communication at synapses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond bone health, calcium is a crucial signaling molecule (IP3 signaling, calmodulin activation) and is required for neurotransmitter release at synapses. Blocking calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal therefore prevents neurotransmitter release into the synapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP hydrolysis depends on magnesium stabilization of ATP, not on calcium entry into nerve terminals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Electron transfer from cytochrome c to oxygen is performed by copper-dependent cytochrome c oxidase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Collagen cross-linking is performed by copper-dependent lysyl oxidase, unrelated to synaptic calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superoxide conversion to hydrogen peroxide is performed by superoxide dismutase, a zinc- and copper-dependent enzyme.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with many years of inadequate dietary calcium intake undergoes bone density testing that shows bone mineral density lower than normal but not yet at the threshold for osteoporosis. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Osteopenia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Osteoporosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Renal osteodystrophy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tetany

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypogonadism

explanation.summary: Long-term hypocalcemia produces osteopenia (lower than normal bone mineral density), which progresses to osteoporosis if untreated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common symptoms of hypocalcemia include tetany and paresthesia acutely, and in the long term osteopenia, defined as lower than normal bone mineral density. Osteopenia eventually progresses to osteoporosis if the calcium deficit is not corrected.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Osteoporosis is the later, more severe end-stage that osteopenia progresses to if untreated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal osteodystrophy is bone pain and fractures from hyperphosphatemia in kidney failure, not dietary calcium deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetany refers to muscle cramps and spasms, an acute symptom of hypocalcemia, not a bone density finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypogonadism is impaired sexual development seen with zinc deficiency in children.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A patient's serum calcium falls, triggering PTH release from the parathyroid glands. Which of the following best describes the effect of PTH on bone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Osteoblasts deposit hydroxyapatite, lowering serum calcium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Osteoclast activity is inhibited, favoring bone formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone releases calcium while retaining all of its phosphate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osteoclasts resorb bone, releasing both calcium and phosphate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bone converts vitamin D to calcitriol by 1-alpha-hydroxylase

explanation.summary: PTH stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption, releasing both calcium and phosphorus into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bones act as a reserve for calcium and phosphate. When bone is broken down by osteoclasts (bone resorption), calcium and phosphorus are both released into the blood. PTH, released in response to hypocalcemia, drives this resorption and is important for controlling both serum calcium and phosphate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Osteoblastic deposition and lowering of calcium describe the effect of calcitonin, which opposes PTH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibition of osteoclasts with bone formation is the action of calcitonin, not PTH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Resorption of hydroxyapatite releases phosphate along with calcium; phosphate is not retained.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity occurs in the kidney, not bone, and is a separate PTH action.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: An in vitro kinase assay shows negligible activity when ATP is supplied alone but robust activity when a particular divalent cation is added. This cation is also essential to cell membrane integrity and potassium balance. Which of the following best describes its interaction with ATP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It hydrolyzes the terminal phosphate bond to release energy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds the adenine ring to prevent enzymatic degradation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is incorporated into the phosphate backbone during synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It displaces protons from ATP, raising its ionized fraction

choices.label: E
choices.text: It coordinates the negatively charged phosphate groups, stabilizing ATP

explanation.summary: Magnesium coordinates the negatively charged phosphate groups of ATP, stabilizing it and increasing its biological activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Magnesium is a macromineral essential to cell membrane integrity and potassium balance, and it has a major role in energy production. It coordinates between the negatively charged phosphate groups of ATP; this binding stabilizes ATP and increases its biological activity, which is why ATP-dependent enzymes need magnesium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Magnesium does not itself hydrolyze ATP; it stabilizes the molecule so enzymes can use it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Magnesium interacts with the phosphate groups, not the adenine ring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Magnesium is not a structural component of ATP; phosphate forms the backbone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proton displacement describes the acidemia effect on albumin-bound calcium, not a magnesium-ATP interaction.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man taking a prescribed diuretic for hypertension develops fatigue, weakness, and a new cardiac arrhythmia. He does not drink alcohol. Serum magnesium is low. Which of the following best explains his hypomagnesemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased tubular filtrate flow decreases reabsorption of magnesium

choices.label: B
choices.text: The diuretic blocks intestinal absorption of dietary magnesium

choices.label: C
choices.text: The diuretic stimulates calcitonin, which promotes magnesium loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: The diuretic shifts magnesium from the extracellular fluid into bone

choices.label: E
choices.text: The diuretic inhibits PTH, which reduces magnesium reabsorption

explanation.summary: Prescribed diuretics cause renal magnesium wasting by increasing filtrate flow and reducing tubular reabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prescribed diuretics can lead to magnesium imbalance just as alcohol does. The increased volume of filtrate flow in the kidney tubules decreases reabsorption of certain macrominerals, and magnesium is particularly vulnerable to this effect, leading to magnesium wasting in the kidneys. Tetany, fatigue and weakness, and cardiac arrhythmias are common symptoms of hypomagnesemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Diuretics act on the kidney tubules, not on intestinal absorption of magnesium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcitonin regulates calcium and is not described as a mediator of magnesium loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diuretic-induced deficiency results from urinary loss, not a shift of magnesium into bone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The relationship runs the other way: magnesium is required for PTH secretion, and PTH does not control magnesium reabsorption.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: Cultured cells grown in a zinc-depleted medium accumulate superoxide radicals. Activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely reduced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytochrome c oxidase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Superoxide dismutase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysyl oxidase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tyrosinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase

explanation.summary: Zinc is a cofactor for superoxide dismutase, which eliminates the superoxide reactive oxygen species.
explanation.whyCorrect: Zinc is a broadly used enzyme cofactor (more than 100 reactions), including the critical reaction of superoxide dismutase, which eliminates the superoxide reactive oxygen species by converting damaging superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Loss of zinc therefore impairs superoxide clearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytochrome c oxidase is copper-dependent and transfers electrons to oxygen in the ETC; it does not clear superoxide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysyl oxidase is copper-dependent and cross-links collagen; it is unrelated to superoxide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tyrosinase is copper-dependent and synthesizes melanin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is copper-dependent and converts dopamine to norepinephrine.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with long-standing Crohn's disease is evaluated for delayed puberty and impaired sexual maturation. He also reports that food has lost its taste, that minor cuts heal slowly, and that he has had several recent infections. Deficiency of which of the following minerals best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copper

choices.label: B
choices.text: Magnesium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zinc

choices.label: D
choices.text: Calcium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phosphorus

explanation.summary: Zinc deficiency in children causes hypogonadism, and other features include loss of taste, delayed wound healing, and immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: A significant hallmark of zinc deficiency in children is impaired sexual development and maturation, referred to as hypogonadism. Other symptoms of zinc deficiency include delayed wound healing, loss of taste, and immunosuppression. Intestinal changes leading to malabsorption, such as Crohn's disease, are an acquired cause of zinc deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Copper deficiency causes anemia and neurologic findings such as ataxia, not hypogonadism and taste loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Magnesium deficiency produces tetany, weakness, and arrhythmias rather than delayed puberty.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium deficiency produces tetany, paresthesia, and reduced bone density, not hypogonadism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphorus abnormalities relate to bone and energy metabolism, not sexual maturation or taste.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: Acrodermatitis enteropathy can arise from either a genetic defect or an acquired condition. Which of the following is a recognized cause of the acquired form?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mutation of the ATP7A gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess dietary copper intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic kidney failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Crohn's disease with malabsorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prescribed diuretic therapy

explanation.summary: Acquired zinc deficiency results from alcoholism or intestinal malabsorption such as IBS, Crohn's disease, or gastric bypass.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acrodermatitis enteropathy has both a genetic basis (a disrupted SLC39A4 gene encoding the ZIP4 transporter) and acquired causes. The acquired form results from alcoholism or intestinal changes leading to malabsorption, including IBS, Crohn's disease, and gastric bypass.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP7A mutation causes Menkes disease, a copper deficiency, not zinc deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess zinc reduces copper absorption, but excess copper is not a described cause of zinc deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kidney failure causes hyperphosphatemia and renal osteodystrophy, not acquired zinc deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diuretics cause renal magnesium wasting, not zinc deficiency.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman who underwent gastric bypass 4 years ago has fatigue and dizziness. Laboratory evaluation confirms copper deficiency. Which of the following best characterizes the anemia most expected in this patient and its mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Megaloblastic macrocytic anemia from impaired DNA synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normocytic or microcytic anemia from impaired iron absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia from free-radical damage to red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microcytic anemia from copper deposition in the marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Macrocytic anemia from loss of ceruloplasmin synthesis

explanation.summary: Copper-deficiency anemia is normocytic or microcytic because copper is directly involved in iron absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Copper is required for maximal iron absorption, so copper deficiency is associated with anemia that is normocytic or microcytic due to copper's direct involvement in iron absorption. In select cases the anemia can be non-megaloblastic macrocytic through unclear mechanisms. Copper deficiency is more common after bariatric surgery, especially gastric bypass, where 8%-16% may have inadequate copper intake.

whyWrongByChoice.A: When macrocytosis occurs in copper deficiency it is non-megaloblastic; impaired DNA synthesis is not the mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolytic anemia is a feature described in select cases of copper toxicity (Wilson's disease), not deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Copper deficiency involves too little copper; there is no marrow copper deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The anemia is attributed to impaired iron absorption, not to loss of ceruloplasmin synthesis.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A laboratory characterizes the distribution of copper in the serum of a healthy adult. Which of the following best describes how most of the circulating copper is carried?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bound to albumin synthesized in the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: As free unbound cations dissolved in the serum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bound to apoceruloplasmin secreted by enterocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complexed with phosphate and bicarbonate anions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bound to ceruloplasmin synthesized in the liver

explanation.summary: Ceruloplasmin, a liver-made protein, carries 60%-90% of the copper in the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Copper is transported in the serum by ceruloplasmin, a protein made in the liver that carries 60%-90% of blood copper. The liver takes copper from the bloodstream and binds it to ceruloplasmin, which is then released to distribute copper to tissues. Apoceruloplasmin is the copper-free precursor, and copper is a cofactor required to convert apoceruloplasmin to ceruloplasmin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin carries calcium, not the majority of copper.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Free unbound copper is a minor fraction in health; it rises abnormally in Wilson's disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Apoceruloplasmin is the copper-free precursor, and ceruloplasmin is made in the liver, not enterocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complexing with phosphate and bicarbonate describes a small fraction of calcium, not copper.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A patient with severe copper deficiency is found to have reduced synthesis of a catecholamine neurotransmitter. Impairment of which of the following copper-dependent conversions best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dopamine to norepinephrine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tyrosine to melanin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Superoxide to hydrogen peroxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cytochrome c to reduced oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lysine to cross-linked collagen

explanation.summary: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is a copper-dependent enzyme that converts dopamine to norepinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Copper is a cofactor for a myriad of critical enzymes, including dopamine beta-hydroxylase, which converts dopamine to norepinephrine. Copper deficiency therefore impairs synthesis of the catecholamine norepinephrine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tyrosinase synthesizes the skin pigment melanin, not a neurotransmitter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide; it is not involved in catecholamine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytochrome c oxidase transfers electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen in the ETC, unrelated to neurotransmitters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysyl oxidase covalently links lysine residues to strengthen collagen fibrils.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: Isolated mitochondria from a copper-deficient animal show markedly reduced oxygen consumption despite adequate substrate and NADH supply. Which of the following enzymes is most likely impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Superoxide dismutase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysyl oxidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tyrosinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cytochrome c oxidase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase

explanation.summary: Copper-dependent cytochrome c oxidase transfers electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen in the electron transport chain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytochrome c oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme that transfers electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen in the ETC. Without adequate copper, this final electron transfer to oxygen is impaired, reducing mitochondrial oxygen consumption even when substrate and NADH are available.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and does not drive mitochondrial oxygen consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen and has no role in the electron transport chain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tyrosinase synthesizes melanin and is unrelated to mitochondrial respiration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts dopamine to norepinephrine, not electrons to oxygen.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with Wilson's disease undergoes liver biopsy, which shows hepatocyte injury with early scarring and extracellular matrix deposition. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of hepatocyte damage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copper binds ceruloplasmin within hepatocytes, forming insoluble deposits

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copper is over-secreted into bile, causing cholestatic injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: Copper generates free radicals that oxidize proteins and lipids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Copper activates calmodulin, triggering hepatocyte apoptosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Copper depletes hepatic zinc, inactivating superoxide dismutase

explanation.summary: Accumulated copper produces free radicals, causing protein and lipid oxidation, lipid peroxidation, and scarring that leads to cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Wilson's disease, abnormal copper accumulation leads to protein and lipid oxidation due to free radical production. Excess copper increases free radicals, lipid peroxidation, and extracellular matrix deposition with scarring. As copper builds up in hepatocytes cirrhosis can occur, and eventually copper leaks into the serum and deposits in tissues throughout the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: In Wilson's disease copper cannot be incorporated into ceruloplasmin; ceruloplasmin is low, and injury is not from ceruloplasmin deposits.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ATP7B defect prevents transport of copper into bile, so bile secretion of copper is reduced, not excessive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calmodulin activation is a calcium signaling process and is not the mechanism of copper toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Copper toxicity injures cells through free radicals directly; zinc depletion is not the described mechanism.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with known Wilson's disease develops new aggression, poor judgment, and impulsive behavior over several months. Copper deposition in which of the following regions best explains these symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frontal lobe

choices.label: B
choices.text: Subcortical cells of the CNS

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eye lens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal tubules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepatocytes

explanation.summary: Frontal lobe copper deposits in Wilson's disease damage executive thinking, judgment, and impulse control.
explanation.whyCorrect: Behavioral changes and neuropsychiatric symptoms in Wilson's disease result from copper deposits in the frontal lobe, which damage high cortical processes like executive thinking, judgment, impulsivity, aggression, and cognition.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Copper accumulation in subcortical cells of the CNS causes dementia, affecting muscle memory and working memory, rather than impulsivity and aggression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Copper deposits in the eye produce Kayser-Fleischer rings, not behavioral change.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal copper deposition does not produce neuropsychiatric symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatocyte copper accumulation causes hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis, not behavioral symptoms.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl is newly diagnosed with Wilson's disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment to lower her copper burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral iron supplementation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copper-binding chelator therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: High-dose vitamin C therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravenous magnesium repletion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Calcitonin administration

explanation.summary: Congenital copper overload is treated with copper binders (chelators); liver transplant can be curative.
explanation.whyCorrect: Wilson's disease is a congenital copper overload treated with copper binders known as chelators, which remove the excess copper. Liver transplant can be curative. Successful treatment prevents progression to cirrhosis and liver failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron supplementation does not remove copper and addresses anemia of copper deficiency, not overload.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin C is relevant to collagen hydroxylation (scurvy), not copper removal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Magnesium repletion treats hypomagnesemia and has no effect on copper accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium and does not affect copper.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy with elevated transaminases is evaluated for Wilson's disease. Serum ceruloplasmin is low, urinary copper excretion is high, and liver biopsy shows high hepatocyte copper. Slit lamp examination shows no Kayser-Fleischer rings. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wilson's disease is excluded because rings are always present

choices.label: B
choices.text: The diagnosis cannot be made until rings appear

choices.label: C
choices.text: The findings indicate Menkes disease rather than Wilson's disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: The diagnosis of Wilson's disease is supported despite absent rings

choices.label: E
choices.text: The low ceruloplasmin argues against copper overload

explanation.summary: Kayser-Fleischer rings support but are not required for the diagnosis of Wilson's disease; their absence does not exclude it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Wilson's disease is diagnosed using serum ceruloplasmin (low), hepatocyte copper (high), and urinary copper excretion (high). Kayser-Fleischer rings, viewed with a slit lamp, further support the diagnosis, but a lack of rings does not exclude it. This patient's laboratory triad establishes the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rings are supportive, not obligatory; their absence does not exclude the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The diagnosis rests on the ceruloplasmin, hepatic copper, and urinary copper findings, not on ring appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Menkes disease produces low whole body, serum, and urinary copper; high urinary and hepatic copper indicate Wilson's disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ceruloplasmin is low in Wilson's disease because copper cannot be incorporated into it despite the overabundance of copper.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: Two children are evaluated for inherited disorders of copper metabolism: one has Wilson's disease and the other has Menkes disease. Which of the following laboratory parameters is expected to be abnormal in the same direction in both patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whole body copper

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free (unbound) serum copper

choices.label: C
choices.text: Urinary copper

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatocyte copper

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum ceruloplasmin

explanation.summary: Ceruloplasmin is low in both Wilson's and Menkes disease, whereas copper measures are high in Wilson's and low in Menkes.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Wilson's disease, whole body copper, free serum copper, and urinary copper are all high, while in Menkes disease all three are low. Serum ceruloplasmin is the one parameter that is low in both: in Wilson's disease because the ATP7B defect prevents copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and in Menkes disease because severe copper deficiency leaves no copper to load onto apoceruloplasmin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Whole body copper is high in Wilson's disease and low in Menkes disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Free unbound serum copper is high in Wilson's disease and low in Menkes disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urinary copper is high in Wilson's disease and low in Menkes disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatocyte copper is high in Wilson's disease, whereas Menkes disease is a state of copper deficiency.

questions.topicName: Basic Nutritional Requirements for Metabolism: Select Minerals

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with Wilson's disease is found to have anemia on routine blood work. Which of the following best describes the type of anemia that may occur in select cases of this copper-overload disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Microcytic anemia due to reduced iron absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrocytic anemia due to unclear mechanisms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia due to copper excess

choices.label: D
choices.text: Megaloblastic anemia due to impaired DNA synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aplastic anemia due to marrow copper deposition

explanation.summary: Hemolytic anemia may occur in select cases of Wilson's disease, in contrast to the iron-absorption anemia of copper deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms of Wilson's disease include behavioral and neuropsychiatric changes, dementia, Kayser-Fleischer rings, hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis, and in select cases hemolytic anemia. Excess copper leaking from the liver into the serum increases free radicals and lipid peroxidation, and hemolytic anemia is the hematologic manifestation described for copper toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Microcytic anemia from reduced iron absorption is the anemia of copper deficiency, the opposite state.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Non-megaloblastic macrocytic anemia through unclear mechanisms is described in select cases of copper deficiency, not overload.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Megaloblastic anemia is not a feature of either copper overload or copper deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aplastic anemia from marrow copper deposition is not a described feature of Wilson's disease.
